news.title: A gut punch in Ohio: Nearly 1,400 laid off at truck factory just days before Trump rally
news.text: SPRINGFIELD, Ohio — Sipping tea from beer mugs with his co-workers, Kyle Bos listed the ways his life is changing.Bos has two daughters, with a third due in January. At the grocery store, five items cost as much as a full cart once did. And on Wednesday, Bos and nearly 1,400 other people were laid off from their jobs at what had been the Navistar truck factory in southwestern Ohio.The layoffs — occurring just three days before President Donald Trump's rally on Saturday at a nearby high school — were large enough to basically erase an entire year of job growth in the greater Dayton, Ohio, area. And they are one reason why Bos, 30, plans to spend the final weeks before the November election canvassing votes for Democrats.Asked how many times he had voted for Trump, Bos held up three tattooed fingers. But he said he's done with the president.'Something has to change politically in this country,' said Bos, a member of the United Auto Workers who identifies as a centrist. 'Seems like it just kept getting worse and worse and worse.'Trump campaigned in this area on SaturdayThis year's election is a test for the working-class coalition that lifted Trump into the White House and gave majorities to Republicans in the House and Senate. The outcome will be decided in places like Dayton, which once sprouted factories because it led America in patents per capita. The Wright brothers' airplane, the cash register, the stepladder and the electric car starter were all invented in this city of 137,000.Trump's blunt talk and status as a celebrity businessman initially helped him around Dayton, where voters sensed that politics as usual had failed them. Republicans secured wins in the larger metro area, but this year, the party is vulnerable with voters who are disgruntled about inflation, the Iran war and a president who seems unsympathetic to their struggles.An Ohio race could help determine control of the Senate. Republican Sen. Jon Husted is facing a challenge from former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown, who is trying to harness that disenchantment as he attempts a comeback two years after losing his seat.Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of living with just 17% approving of his handling of the issue. Trump didn't talk about grocery prices or gas prices or layoffs at his Saturday night rally in Vandalia, part of what he says will be a 32-day marathon of rallies to try to convince the public that the economy is better than they think.'The fake news media, they refuse to talk about our record-setting numbers. So tonight, if you don't mind, I'm going to do it myself,' he told the rally.Trump has largely sneered at concerns about affordability, but he is promising to give people $5,000 checks if Republicans win the House and Senate next month — something Bos said he found offensive.'It feels like a bribe, a slap in the face, and, like, that we're all ignorant,' Bos said.When factory work moved abroad, Republicans gained tractionThe Dayton area has shed about half of its 90,000 factory jobs since 1990, according to federal data, after the North American Free Trade Agreement shifted many jobs to Mexico where auto parts could be made more cheaply. That trend accelerated after China joined the World Trade Organization.As steady paychecks vanished, drug addiction and crime increased. Things seemed to hit bottom after the 2008 financial crisis, prompting Phil Plummer — who was then Montgomery County Sheriff — to enter politics.'My jail was 40% drug addicts, 50% mental health patients, 10% criminals,' said Plummer, who has been a Republican state representative since 2019. 'We got it upside down — that's what drove me to the state house.'Plummer, the Montgomery County Republican chairman, is now on the ballot for the Ohio state Senate and stressed that Trump has been what keeps the GOP's coalition of businesses and working-class families together.In recent years, the local economy has improved as the Wright-Patterson Air Force Base expanded, now directly employing 38,000 people. The base's innovations have attracted new aerospace companies to the area, including Joby Aviation, the Sierra Nevada Corporation and Electra.Trump pointed to the $850 million investment by aircraft maker Electra — along with a new project in Ohio from Stellantis and a Friday announcement from Bayer for a $2.2 billion drug plant near Columbus — as evidence his policies were creating jobs.Dayton rebounded because Republicans and Democrats alike saw the value coming out of Wright-Patterson over the past two decades, said Jeff Hoagland, CEO of the Dayton Development Coalition.'In economic development, it takes time, and you have got to give it a little bit of time to bake, and then once it does, then you're going to have something special,' Hoagland said.Even as Dayton recovers, its politicians say this election is about inflationDowntown Dayton has added lofts for housing, and the historic Dayton Arcade complex with its glass dome and mosaic-tiled floors has been renovated into shops, an art gallery and eateries.On Monday, the gallery echoed with the sounds of an acoustic guitar and flute during a fundraiser for Rose Lounsbury, a former schoolteacher who, for the second time, is running as a Democrat for state representative.The guests radiated optimism that Democrats might pick up a U.S. Senate seat, a governorship and enough spots in the Ohio House of Representatives to end a Republican supermajority.'There is a gap between what people want and what they feel is available,' Lounsbury said. 'People don't want to live a life of subsistence. They want to live the middle-class dream and they feel it's not available like it once was.'Lounsbury's Republican opponent, State Rep. Andrea White, was in the state capital, Columbus, during the past week, where she helped lead a push to pass a temporary suspension of the state gas tax of 38.5 cents per gallon to offer some relief at the pump.White said the Republican-led state government has helped to cushion the blow of inflation by flattening the state income tax and reining in property tax hikes.'The concept is, put it back in the hands of the people who pay the taxes — so they have more of their own money,' White said.No tax on overtime doesn't help these factory workersThe White House said Trump's tax cuts and trade deals have helped Ohio. But the experiences at what had been the Navistar plant show that policies that were supposed to help the working class were not enough.His broad tariffs failed to boost demand and the plant's former owner, International Motors, chose to offload the facility. And Trump's major legislative achievement — the One Big Beautiful Bill — contributed little to people's take-home pay, even as it temporarily stripped taxes from tips and overtime.'We weren't getting a lot of overtime because of the economy,' said Marianne Donnelly, who drove a forklift at the factory. 'There just wasn't any to be had, very little to be had.'Meanwhile, costs have kept climbing. Donnelly said she buys marked-down beef, pork and chicken and stows them in her freezer. She canceled her subscriptions to The Columbus Dispatch and The Washington Post newspapers, along with some streaming services.Laid-off workers like Donnelly say they expect to be rehired in six to 12 months by Roshel, a Canadian manufacturer of armored vehicles that is buying the plant. Roshel said in a statement that it's 'working with everyone involved not only to protect the current workforce, but to more than double it over the coming years through a phased process.'Laid-off workers are looking for hopeOn the Monday before the layoffs, Morgan Hughes and JoJo Burkhard were knocking on doors in Kettering, a Dayton suburb named after the inventor of the electric car starter. They were trying to convince union members and retirees to vote for Democrats.The Navistar job had helped Hughes, 35, buy a house at age 21 and work alongside her father.When her hours were first cut, Hughes moonlighted for DoorDash and got a real estate license. On her wrist, she has a tattoo of a cross and the words 'Be Still And Know,' a reference to Psalm 46:10, which speaks to how faith in God can overcome fear.Hughes said that what union members and retirees want is to be heard after feeling ignored by politicians. Burkhard said inflation and the economy have made it easier to swing voters to their side.'It isn't a hard pitch at all,' she said. 'And even if they don't want to stay Democratic long-term, they'll at least give the candidates a chance this election, which could be a turning point for us.'After a morning of talking to voters, the pair settled down at a Chinese restaurant for some potstickers, and the weight of the week hit them.Burkhard cracked open a fortune cookie and tears began to well up. The layoffs meant no work for her, her boyfriend and her mother — and the words in small print almost seemed prophetic. She said she needed the hope they conveyed.Her fortune read: 'You'll find your inner strength to overcome challenges.

news.title: Kevin Warsh Was Confirmed as Fed Chair in the Most Divisive Vote in Federal Reserve History, 54-45. Here's Why That Split Still Matters Now That He's Raised Rates for the First Time Since 2023.
news.text:
Kevin Warsh's confirmation vote in the Senate in May 2026 was the most divisive ever for a Federal Reserve chair, according to CNBC. The 45 senators who voted against his confirmation likely feared that the new Fed chair would end up trying to bend the Federal Reserve's policies to the preferences of the White House, even at the expense of the national economy, as well as the prestige and credibility of the central bank. Every Republican voted yes, as did one Democrat, Sen. John Fetterman.

But at its mid-September meeting, the Fed raised rates. The S&P 500 (^GSPC +0.73%) took it in stride, climbing very slightly in the following weeks. So, what does that hike prove about the independence that 45 no votes doubted?

This could be the first hike of a few

Warsh faces a credibility issue that he has just started to address, and it isn't just the Democrats that he's trying to build a reputation with.

Before Warsh's confirmation, the Justice Department opened a probe of his predecessor, Jerome Powell.

A judge later ruled that the probe was a pretext, and it was dropped in April. The investigation began after President Donald Trump took issue with Powell's oversight of renovations to the Federal Reserve headquarters. He also publicly castigated Powell for failing to cut interest rates.

The president had demanded rates of "1% or less" and has generally called for rates to be among the lowest in the world -- an approach that would likely be foolhardy at the moment, given that Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation ran at 3.4% in August 2026, per Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) data.

Why should investors care?

Warsh raised rates over Trump's public objections, but Trump says he told Warsh to vote with the board anyway, so the hike might not prove much. The real test of Warsh's mettle will come if he judges that high inflation justifies another hike.

For investors, Warsh's independence matters because inflation expectations determine interest rates, which in turn affect the valuations of stocks and other assets. If people believe that the Fed will cut rates on command, bond investors will demand higher yields to compensate for the risk. Higher yields reduce the present value of future corporate profits, which hits growth stocks hardest.

The next test for Warsh will be at the Fed's Oct. 27-28 meeting.

If inflation remains on the hot side and the Fed continues to hold out against White House pressure for lower rates, the 45 no votes on the confirmation will look misplaced. On the other hand, if Trump can make enough noise to force the Fed's hand, investors will need to buckle up and prepare for a world in which the central bank is uninterested in maintaining the purchasing power of its currency when it's politically inconvenient to do so.

And most likely, that would be incredibly bad for the market as a whole, though inflation-resistant assets would probably perform quite well.
news.summary: The new Federal Reserve chair still has a lot to prove, and political factors are making that harder.

news.title: 'Easy Way Or Hard Way': Trump Says US To Decide Next Step On Iran, Claims Tehran 'Decimated'
news.text:
US President Donald Trump on Saturday said Washington would decide its next course of action on Iran, warning that the outcome would come either the "easy way or the hard way" while claiming that Tehran had been "decimated".
"We have a decision that I'll make about Iran. Iran's been decimated. So the only question is, it'll either be the easy way or the hard way. We'll have it the easy way or the hard way," Trump told reporters outside the White House.
ALSO READ: Two Iranian UN Delegation Members 'Kicked Out' Of US After Ignoring Order To Leave
Trump Withholds Details On Iran Strategy
Trump did not disclose what action his administration could take against Iran or provide a timeline for his next steps.
His latest remarks came as he said the situation was progressing favourably and maintained that Iran was not doing well.
A day earlier, Trump was asked about his strategy for Iran and indicated that revealing details would attract significant attention.
"If I told you, you'd have a major story, right? But you'll see. Working out very well. Iran is not doing well," Trump said on Friday.
The US President has continued to withhold details of his forthcoming actions concerning Iran.
ALSO READ: Netanyahu Invites PM Modi, Captain Smit Machchhar To Light Israel Independence Day Flame
Trump Says War Could End 'Very Quickly'
Earlier, Trump had said the war with Iran would end "very quickly" and predicted that oil prices would fall sharply once the hostilities ended.
Speaking to reporters in Texas, Trump said Iran faced a decisive choice over how the conflict would conclude. "Iran will very soon be ending one way or the other," Trump said.
"It’ll either just say, look, they have 301 per cent inflation. They have no money; they have no currency. Their military has been defeated, their navy is gone, their air force is gone, everything's gone," he added.
Reiterating that the war would end soon, the US President further stated: "And, one way or the other, it’s going to end very quickly. And when that ends, oil prices are going to drop like a rock."

news.title: Trump Taunts Kaitlan Collins in Wild Red State Rally Attack
news.text:
Donald Trump can’t get Kaitlan Collins out of his head. 

The president took time out of a MAGA rally speech in Ohio on Saturday night to bash the CNN star, who was in attendance. 

“She’s such an unhappy person,” the 80-year-old president declared. “She never smiles. She’s a very unhappy person,” he repeated, eventually goading the crowd into booing the journalist. 

In the past, Trump has called Collins “stupid,” “nasty,” “crazy,” and “average.”

Collins, 34, has seemed to shrug off Trump’s relentless attacks. She went on air this week with a mug placed prominently on her desk during her show, The Source, emblazoned with what appeared to be a subtle message for the president: “America Needs Nasty Women.”

Social media users quickly set about trying to wipe the smile off Trump’s face. “The most powerful snowflake in the world still can’t cope with being challenged by a woman,” wrote X user Anna Komsa.

Someone accused Trump of having “Kaitlan Derangement Syndrome (KDS),” while another warned: “Look at this predator making a woman feel uncomfortable in a crowd full of MAGA a------s booing at her. Is her life in danger here?”

The Daily Beast has reached out to the White House and CNN for comment. 

The White House Rapid Response Team tweeted during the rally that “Ohio is not happy with Fake news CNN and Kaitlan Collins.”

Trump has a reputation for being particularly vile when it comes to attacking female journalists who challenge him.

In 2015, shortly after he launched his first bid for president, he was asked during a candidates’ debate by then-Fox News host Megyn Kelly about his history of viciously attacking women. “You call women you don’t like fat pigs, dogs, slobs, and disgusting animals,” she pointed out. Trump snapped back with a rejoinder he apparently thought was hilarious: “Only Rosie O’Donnell.”

The president took time out of a MAGA rally speech in Ohio on Saturday night to bash the CNN star, who was in attendance. 

Trump insisted that Collins “never smiles,” despite the countless hours of footage showing her doing exactly that on TV and at public events.

news.title: World News | India, Cyprus Hold First Joint Maritime Committee Meeting
news.text:
Nicosia [Cyprus], October 4 (ANI): Marking a significant milestone in bilateral relations, India and Cyprus held the first meeting of their Joint Maritime Committee (JMC) in Limassol, which was co-chaired by Venkatesapathy S, Joint Secretary (International Cooperation) in the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, alongside Theodoulos Mesimeris, Acting Permanent Secretary in the Shipping Deputy Ministry of Cyprus, as announced by the High Commission of India in Nicosia on Saturday.

"The first India-Cyprus Joint Maritime Committee (JMC) met under the 2017 bilateral Agreement on Merchant Shipping," the High Commission stated on X, calling it a new chapter in India-Cyprus maritime cooperation. The meeting was held on September 29.

Also Read | 'One Last Fight Left in Me': Flydubai Captain Smit Machchhar Recounts Co-Pilot Attack to Benjamin Netanyahu.

The diplomatic delegation from New Delhi, which featured India's High Commissioner to Cyprus, Manish, alongside officials from the Nicosia mission and Deependra Singh Bisena, Deputy Director General in the Directorate General of Maritime Administration, engaged extensively with Cypriot authorities and industry leaders across a four-day itinerary spanning September 28 to October 1.

The talks covered maritime education and training, investment opportunities in both sectors, the exchange of policies and strategies as best practices, and cooperation on matters of mutual interest at the International Maritime Organization (IMO).

Also Read | USD 5,000 for Every American Adult? Donald Trump's Midterm Pledge, Cost and What Polls Say.

Further strengthening institutional ties, the visiting delegation held structured interactions with the Cyprus Shipping Chamber, premier maritime enterprises, the Cyprus Ports Authority, and the Cyprus Marine and Maritime Institute, complemented by an official site visit to the Port of Limassol.

"Opportunities explored included maritime services, shipping finance, ship repair and recycling, seafarer training and welfare, and green shipping," the High Commission stated.

Looking ahead to upcoming bilateral exchanges, both sides reviewed logistical frameworks for the scheduled visit of the Cypriot Shipping Deputy Minister to India, accompanied by a high-level trade delegation, ahead of a prominent Maritime Business Forum slated for Mumbai in November 2026 to catalyse joint ventures and capital investments. 

"The meeting forms part of the India-Cyprus Joint Action Plan and reflects the shared commitment of Hon'ble Prime Minister Mr Narendra Modi and H.E. President Mr Nikos Christodoulides to deepen bilateral cooperation," the High Commission added.

These strategic developments underline a consistent intensification of high-level diplomatic and economic dialogues between the two nations in recent times. (ANI)

ANI brings the latest news on Politics and Current Affairs in India & around the World, Sports, Health, Fitness, Entertainment, & News. The views appearing in the above post do not reflect the opinions of LatestLY)

Co-chaired by senior officials, the talks explored green shipping, training, and maritime finance ahead of an upcoming business forum in Mumbai.

news.title: 325m barrels of emergency oil released, says IEA
news.text:
PARIS: The International Energy Agency said on Saturday that member countries had so far released 325 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products from strategic reserves, from 400 million barrels promised in March.

The update came a day after G7 countries, in coordination with the IEA, agreed to immediately release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns caused by fallout from the US-Iran war.

The G7 did not say whether the 100 million barrels included the outstanding 75 million barrels from the March IEA commitment, or came on top of that.

The US government of President Donald Trump has been pressuring allies to release diesel reserves to ease a spike in prices for the fuel, being felt in America and elsewhere.

Trump says US will soon fill its strategic oil stockpile ‘for nothing’

Restricted diesel supplies are one of the consequences of the war in the Middle East, where Iran has been throttling ship traffic through the Strait of Hormuz in retaliation for US and Israeli attacks.

Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries, part of the fightback against Moscow’s strikes, have also affected the market.

March pledge

The IEA said in a statement on Saturday that “around 325 million barrels of the IEA collective action announced on March 11 have so far been released, representing over 80 per cent of the 400 million barrels originally pledged in the action”.

The March pledge was offered up by the IEA’s 32 member countries, a grouping that includes all the G7 nations: Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and the US.

The G7 countries on Friday agreed to release over the next four months 100 million barrels of oil and oil-derivative products, “including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days”.

They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between them — heading off a threat Washington had brandished, and which Trump later said would not be enacted.

In a related development, President Trump said on Friday that the US would soon fill its strategic petroleum reserves.

“We’re going to be filling up very shortly our strategic reserves, for nothing,” Trump said at a rally in Mobile, Alabama. He offered no additional details.

news.title: Tehran’s wartime billboards mock Trump, boast of victory
news.text:
TEHRAN: Huge billboards on the walls of Tehran mocking US President Donald Trump and depicting American drones under the boot of an Iranian soldier are providing a chronicle of Iran’s war with the United States and Israel.

AFP got rare access to a team producing the billboards with anti-US messaging for prominent locations in Tehran where they are seen daily by large crowds of passers-by, including the city’s famed Valiasr Square.

Khaneh-ye Tarrahan, or Designers’ House, created a towering portrayal of Trump’s lips sewn and his mouth muzzled by the Strait of Hormuz waterway at the center of the Iran war, accompanied by the words “At the breaking point.”

“When news breaks, the team mobilizes: ideas are generated, the graphic designers are briefed and we collaborate,” said Mostafa Kafaei, 32, who manages the studio.

As he spoke, people worked on projects at several desks in the office.

It features a whiteboard for brainstorming, while photos of martyrs and ideas adorn the hallway wall.

Kafaei’s studio, which includes a dedicated media-monitoring team, works under one of the country’s biggest state-run media conglomerates.

The billboards are sponsored by the government and used to convey its messages far and wide.

One from a different studio shows Trump trapped inside a magician’s box, clutching a Coca-Cola and a hamburger with the words: “Blink, you’re gone!“

The billboard references a July incident in Turkiye where Trump was smuggled from Air Force One to a different aircraft on a catering truck due to a security threat.

“Speed has become a top priority,” said Kafaei, with urgent posters turned around in just a few days by teams of up to around eight people.

Most of their work is created in Photoshop, he said, adding that the team is “highly proficient in AI,” using “various AI engines, such as ChatGPT and Nano Banana” as part of the production process.

Another towering billboard recently put up in Tehran shows an Iranian soldier stepping on a US underwater drone, depicting a recent “Hormuz catch” by Iran’s Revolutionary Guards and bragging that “Business is good.”

Iran has blockaded commercial shipping through the Hormuz strait since the war began in late February with US-Israeli strikes on the Islamic republic, while the US military has upheld a counterblockade of Iran’s ports.

A different advert shows a mythical warrior standing in raging seas as US warships burn, along with a message reading “Satan’s army will drown in the Arabian Gulf.”

Riffing off the cover of Nirvana’s “Nevermind” album, another depicts Trump grasping at a dollar bill underwater, next to the words “GREAT VICTORY! Strait of Hormuz.”

“There was some initial hesitation about whether to feature such a large image of Trump’s face on the Valiasr mural,” Kafaei said of the image with Trump’s lips sewn up, which appeared in May as the strategic trade route became central to the conflict.

But “the overall assessment was that the final piece would be exceptionally powerful,” he said.

When asked why the US leader featured on so many billboards, Kafaei said Trump “is a media personality... We respond in kind whenever he takes action in that space.”

Comparing it to a battlefield scenario with an adversary “constantly firing at us,” the studio chief said “we keep a close watch on our opponent and respond accordingly.”

‘Satan’s wedding gift’ 

Large billboards glorifying Iran, its former supreme leader Ali Khamenei, killed at the start of the war, and allies like slain Hezbollah chief Hassan Nasrallah have also appeared around the city.

Kafaei said the billboards helped many people who “may not be politically minded” to grasp “the overall context of what is going on in the country.”

Retiree Mahmoudreza Rezaei, 53, recalled seeing a billboard that referred to “Satan’s wedding gift” — a message he understood to be directed at Trump after an alleged US attack in the country’s south last month that killed several people at a wedding ceremony.

“It kept me pondering for a few minutes, trying to decipher the meaning,” Rezaei said. “It had a bit of a riddle-like quality.”

Sahar Jahedi, 24, who works in a pharmacy, said she was captivated by the billboard of Trump trapped in the magician’s box, which went up in central Tehran’s Jomhouri Square.

While “so many people are currently struggling just to survive, they may not have the time” to follow the news, she said.

“Billboards like this... can play a significant role in keeping more people informed about current events.”

news.title: Iran war to end ‘very soon’: Trump
news.text:
Says there is ‘nobody to deal with’ in Tehran• US senator urges Congress to cut funding for military action• Pentagon study to examine future warfare after operations against Iran• IRGC commander says Iran has technological ‘surprises’ for adversaries• Two oil tankers struck by unidentified projectiles near Hormuz

WASHINGTON: US President Donald Trump has said the war with Iran could end “very soon”, while questioning whom Washington could negotiate with in Teh-ran and reiterating that Iran must never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.

Speaking at a rally in Alabama, Trump said there appeared to be no clear counterpart in Tehran with whom Washington could negotiate, Al Jazeera reported.

“I don’t know who the hell to deal with. There’s nobody to deal with,” he said, bef-ore adding: “Knock knock, nobody home.”

Trump said the war would end soon “one way or the other”. It’s “gonna end very soon, and probably right after the midterms”, he said.

However, his remarks came as fresh attacks were reported on commercial shipping around the Strait of Hormuz and concerns persisted over a possible expansion of the US military presence in the Middle East.

Tankers attacked near Hormuz

Two oil tankers were struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz region, according to the United Kingdom Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), in the latest threat to shipping through the key waterway.

The first attack caused “a small fire and blackout onboard”, the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) agency said Friday, adding that the fire was later extinguished.

There were no reported casualties or environmental impact, it added.

The vessel, which was exiting the strait, was able to resume its journey, UKMTO said, without specifying the ship’s ports of origin and destination.

Hours later, another crude oil tanker reported being struck by an “unknown projectile” east of Oman, with all crew safe and no environmental damage reported, according to the UKMTO.

The agency said authorities were investigating the incidents.

Senator urges funding cutoff

Meanwhile, US Senator Chris Van Hollen accused the Trump administration of preparing to expand the US military presence in the Middle East and urged Congress to cut off funding for what he called an “illegal war of choice” against Iran, Anadolu reported.

“The president, who continues to hide service member casualties, is now sending up to another 10,000 troops to his illegal war of choice in Iran,” Van Hollen wrote on X.

“When Trump says he’s planning on renewing his war next month, believe him. Congress must cut off funding,” he added.

His remarks came amid reports that the Pentagon was preparing to deploy a third aircraft carrier strike group and additional Marine Corps ships to the region as Trump considered resuming strikes on Iran after the US midterm elections in early November.

Pentagon studies future warfare

At the same time, Washington is examining lessons from its military operations against Iran as part of a broader study of future warfare.

The Pentagon has commissioned “Project Meridian: The Future of Warfare” to examine future battlefields and identify the weapons, technologies and operational concepts US forces would require to maintain an advantage.

A Pentagon memo cited US operations in Iran as demonstrating what it called the “unmatched technological prowess” of US forces.

The project will examine rapidly developing technologies including artificial intelligence, autonomy, directed energy, robotics and biotechnology, which the Pentagon says could significantly alter the character of warfare. It has warned that Washington cannot take its existing technological advantages for granted.

Meanwhile, Iran has responded with its own claims of technological advances.

IRGC Deputy Commander-in-Chief Maj Gen Mostafa Izadi said Iranian armed forces had made major progress in ground, air, air-defence and naval capabilities and had further technological “surprises” in store for their adversaries, according to Press TV.

“The armed forces are using various technologies, some of which have been employed on the battlefield and others will be utilised in the future,” he said.

Hamas calls on US, mediators to prevent Israel from attacking Gaza during ceasefire

BEIRUT october 3

Palestinian movement Hamas on Saturday called on the US administration and the other mediators in its talks with Israel to prevent Israel from using the ceasefire agreement on the Gaza Strip as a cover to continue strikes on Palestinian territory.

"We call on the mediators and the US administration not to allow [Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin] Netanyahu to use the ceasefire agreement as a cover to continue his mass killings," Hamas said in a statement.

Earlier on Saturday, an Israeli airstrike on a residential building in Gaza City killed at least five people, including four women, local medical services said. The Israeli army did not comment on the strike.

On October 9, 2025, Israel and Hamas, with the mediation of Egypt, Qatar, the United States, and Turkey, agreed to implement the first phase of the peace plan presented by US President Donald Trump. The following day, a ceasefire went into effect in the Gaza Strip. news.title: Sanaa, Riyadh rattled by strikes as war widens
news.text:
Houthis say Saudi aircraft carried out 26 strikes on Yemen capital, claim attack on Aramco facility in south of Riyadh• Trump’s top national security aides meet secretly on Yemen, Iran

SANAA: Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis showed no signs of abating on Saturday, with the Houthis saying the kingdom had launched dozens of strikes on capital Sanaa, while flames and smoke were seen rising from a facility belonging to Saudi oil giant Aramco, south of Riyadh.

While Houthis later said they attacked an Aramco facility with ballistic missiles and drones, there was no immediate confirmation from Saudi Arabia. The foes have traded strikes since the Houthis seized all of Yemen’s Red Sea coast and took control of the Bab al-Mandab strait in a lightning offensive.

US media outlet Axios reported earlier on Friday that US President Donald Trump’s top cabinet members “met secretly at the presidential retreat at Camp David to discuss the Saudi-Houthi conflict in Yemen and next steps in the Iran war”. Vice President Vance chaired the meeting, the news outlet reported, citing people familiar with the matter.

Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV reported that Saudi aircraft hit Sanaa with 26 strikes, after earlier reporting “Saudi aggression” against the Yemeni capital, without providing details on the targets or casualties.

Two AFP correspondents in Sanaa reported hearing loud explosions and seeing warplanes firing missiles on the city.

In neighbouring Saudi Arabia, flames and smoke were seen rising on Saturday afternoon from a facility belonging to state-owned oil giant Aramco south of Riyadh, an AFP journalist said, although both the Houthis and Saudi authorities had yet to comment.

The circumstances remained unclear, though the Houthis have claimed several attacks on facilities belonging to Aramco, majority-owned by the Saudi state, in recent months.

The journalist reported seeing firefighters attempting to extinguish a blaze at the energy giant’s Riyadh refinery, located south of the capital, while ambulances and police vehicles were stationed near the facility.

Al-Masirah TV earlier on Saturday also reported missile strikes on the telecommunications network in Yemen’s northwestern governorate of Saada, one of the group’s strongholds.

It comes after the Houthis said that Saudi Arabia bombed the Yemeni capital itself on Thursday night for the first time since renewed fighting broke out between the two sides in July.

The health ministry in Sanaa claims 72 people have been killed and 125 wounded in Saudi attacks on Yemen since the escalation began, Al Jazeera reports citing the Al Masirah news outlet.

Hunger warning

After several years of calm, Yemen was plunged back into civil war that month, pitting the Houthis, who control most of northwest Yemen including Sanaa, against Yemen’s internationally recognised government.

The government, based in the city of Aden, controls much of the country’s south and east — a region that is larger but much less populated.

Hostilities were reignited after four years of a fragile truce when Iran sent a plane to Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation.

The flight did not seek authorisation from Saudi Arabia, contravening a practice in place for a decade.

Riyadh retaliated with strikes on Sanaa airport, and in response the Houthis attacked Saudi territory for the first time since 2022.

Since then, fighting has intensified with the Houthis launching a lightning offensive in which they seized control of coastal regions along the Bab al-Mandab strait.

They have also struck multiple Saudi targets including oil infrastructure and the capital Riyadh while also announcing a naval blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea.

Appalling conditions

The renewed fighting has worsened the already appalling humanitarian conditions in Yemen, one of the world’s poorest countries, with the World Food Programme warning on Friday that three-quarters of the population was unable to meet its basic food needs.

Fighting in recent days has centred on Taiz, where dozens of combatants were reported killed on Friday by sources on both sides.

The Houthis reported 55 of their fighters had been killed while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died.

The battle for Taiz is taking place on several fronts, including highlands overlooking coastal areas recently seized by the Houthis.

While the Houthis have conquered swathes of territory, they have yet to wrest control of Taiz city, which is Yemen’s third-largest after Sanaa and Aden.

The Houthis also on Friday said Saudi Arabia had launched 94 strikes against areas under their control in the past 24 hours.

Saudi authorities meanwhile reported a Houthi projectile had damaged a school in the city of Najran near the Yemen border.

Published in Dawn, October 4th, 2026

news.title: Trump tariffs a mixed bag for U.S. auto industry
news.text: New York - U.S. President Donald Trump has claimed a “roaring comeback” in American auto manufacturing following aggressive trade policy, but analysts view the cumulative impact as more of a mixed bag.Since Trump returned to the White House, General Motors, Toyota, Ford and other carmakers have announced plans to expand U.S. plants or shift production from overseas to make use of underutilized factories, as the industry navigated measures such as a 25% levy on imported autos.But as the president’s allies in the Republican Party look ahead to midterm elections in November, the gains to the U.S. carmaker profile look more incremental than decisive, and are accompanied by a drag in spending in some cases due to trade uncertainty.
news.summary: Trump has claimed a "roaring comeback" in U.S. auto manufacturing following aggressive trade policy, but analysts say its more of a mixed bag.

news.title: Trump, campaigning in Ohio, says the midterms will bring a ‘big surprise’
news.text: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate. “I think we’re going to have a big surprise, because they don’t know what’s happening,” Trump said while speaking onstage inside a high school gymnasium near Dayton. “Just get out and vote,” Trump added. “If you do that, we’re going to win, and we’re going to win big. And we’re going to shove it up their ass.” The visit, part of what White House officials have told NBC News will be a push through at least 17 states between now and Nov. 3, was aimed at boosting incumbent Sen. Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy, the GOP nominee for governor. Trump, who won Ohio three times by comfortable margins, opened his speech with praise for both before moving into broader remarks to promote himself and his administration. He also offered support for local Rep. Mike Turner and for several House candidates in attendance, including Derek Merrin, the Republican running against longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur in northwest Ohio. Husted’s bid to keep the Senate seat — which he was appointed to after JD Vance was elected vice president — has in particular become a subject of concern among Republicans in Ohio and Washington. In August, the National Republican Senatorial Committee warned in a memo that Husted’s past enthusiasm for building data centers was hurting his campaign. Others have expressed worries that Husted, who has long wanted to be governor, has not put his full heart into the race. The battle is one of the most expensive and competitive Senate races in the country this fall. Along with a handful of other key contests, the clash between Husted and Brown could determine partisan control of the chamber. This week, Senate Leadership Fund, a super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune of South Dakota, poured another $14 million into Ohio to prop up Husted, bringing the group’s investment in the state to $93 million. “Senator Jon Husted votes to put Ohio first, and he votes all the time,” Trump said before relating conversations he’s had with Thune and others: “They think he’s phenomenal.” The high school gym where Trump spoke Saturday night was a smaller venue than has been typical for his rallies. The home court of the Butler High School Aviators seats up to 5,000. There were several stretches of empty seats in upper bleachers as Trump took the stage — and many more by the time he finished speaking 93 minutes later. In Ohio and elsewhere, Republicans are wrestling with how to win at a time when polls show Trump and the war in Iran are highly unpopular and when voters most loyal to Trump might stay home because he’s not on the ballot. “As a lifelong Republican who’s voted in every election since I was 18 and in every primary election as a Republican, I have real concerns that we’re going to be able to turn out the every-four-year Trump voter,” Nick Owens, a former GOP chair in Ohio’s Brown County and former member of the state Board of Education, told NBC News last month. “I have real concerns that those voters just will not come to the polls.” Trump acknowledged that dynamic explicitly Saturday and repeated an argument he’s been making on the campaign trail this fall. “When I run, we win,” Trump said. “But for some reason, when I don’t run, they draw 44% less people. So what I’m going to do is ask you to just pretend that I’m running, because if we do, and if you draw the people, you’re going to win, and we’re going to win big.” Husted, speaking to reporters before the rally, described Trump as a unique asset in his race. “Well, he won Ohio by 11 points in the last election, and if we get those same voters to turn out in this election, we’ll win,” Husted said. Alex Triantafilou, the Ohio GOP chair, told NBC News that the rally was “hugely important” in the effort to motivate those low-propensity, Trump-loyal voters. “We know in Ohio that if we turn out the same electorate that we turned out in 2024, that we’ll win every race,” Triantafilou said in an interview. “Nobody speaks to that crowd better than President Trump.” The Saturday rally included a cameo from Jon Gruden, the former NFL coach who years ago was a teammate of Husted’s on the University of Dayton football team. “Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend,” an animated Gruden told the audience. “He was a great player. … He will never quit on you or anybody.” Trump marveled about Husted’s football-playing days, of which he said he was unaware until hearing about them from Gruden. “Nobody told me you were a great athlete,” Trump said, before taking a jab at his Democratic rival: “And Brown was not — he was not an athlete. That guy can’t tie his shoes.” For its part Saturday, the Brown team sent a mobile billboard linking Husted’s support for the war in Iran to higher gas prices through Dayton and on the streets near the rally. “Jon Husted has turned his back on working families — he’s only looking out for his billionaire buddies and special interests,” Brown said in a statement from his campaign. Ohio also is home to what polls show is a close race to succeed term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. Ramaswamy faces Democrat Amy Acton, a physician who served as the state’s health director under DeWine. Ohioans have not elected a Democrat as governor in 20 years, but at a time when high prices rate as a top-of-mind concern for voters, there are questions about the billionaire Ramaswamy’s appeal, especially in the rural parts of the state. Ramaswamy, like Husted, addressed the crowd early during the rally, and Trump invited both to return to the stage during his speech for additional remarks. Trump introduced Ramaswamy by noting how he had briefly run against him for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination. “He was a nasty guy,” Trump said of Ramaswamy. “But you know what? He was smart. He loves the state. He’s actually got a great heart.” Compared with Husted, Ramaswamy was otherwise less of a focus of Trump’s remarks. Trump, for example, criticized Senate Democrats who this week blocked Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, which aims to rein in higher utility costs associated with power-hungry data centers. Republicans, Trump said, are “taking historic action to ensure that Big Tech data centers benefit local communities.” Trump then made the argument for data centers, despite the fears it could be a losing issue for Husted. “We want them,” Trump said. “Look, there’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China.” Trump also recited the lyrics to the 1968 Al Wilson song “The Snake” — a recurring, crowd-pleasing bit in his rally speeches — with a new, localized twist. Trump dedicated the song, which he uses as an allegory to trusting communities that welcome immigrants, to nearby Springfield, Ohio. The city became a flashpoint in the 2024 presidential election after Trump repeated the unsubstantiated and racially charged claim that Haitian immigrants in the city were eating dogs and pets. At another point, the crowd broke into chants of “four more years” for the term-limited president. “I’d love to do the four-more-year thing,” Trump responded in a teasing tone before suggesting that the press would overplay his remarks. “We’re driving them totally crazy,” Trump said, referring to the media. “But I love doing it. I love being with you. I really do.”
news.summary: VANDALIA, Ohio — President Donald Trump rallied Saturday for Republicans in Ohio’s competitive races for Senate and governor, predicting that the party will defy expectations in a choppy midterm election climate.
news.author: Henry J. Gomez

news.title: Trump names DNI chief Jay Clayton as AI czar to lead new White House task force: Report
news.text:
ANIJay Clayton has been appointed as the AI czar by Donald Trump to lead a new panel.

US President Donald Trump has appointed Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton as the administration's AI czar, the Wall Street Journal reported on Saturday, citing an interview with Clayton.Clayton, who was appointed intelligence chief in August, will lead a new White House panel tasked with reporting within 120 days on the risks and opportunities posed by AI, the newspaper said."The president asked that a group be put together," which the administration refers to as the "Super Intelligence Force," to ensure the US remains a leader in advanced AI while protecting Americans' interests, Clayton told the Journal, adding that "the risk of not being first is high."The safety of AI has become a major issue in recent weeks, with some researchers warning that people building the technology believe it could kill humans within a decade. Several Democratic and Republican lawmakers have responded with alarm and calls for more action.Trump has appeared to take a light touch toward AI regulation, arguing that excessive oversight could weaken competitiveness against China. He said on Tuesday that he does not want to work with Chinese President Xi Jinping on governing AI technology.Live EventsClayton's panel will review AI-related risks and current government reporting mechanisms for breaches, hacks and other incidents, and recommend ways to strengthen federal-response capabilities under existing authorities, the Journal said, citing the task force's charter.This is the second time Trump has named an adviser to oversee AI-related decisions across the administration. Venture capitalist David Sacks held the AI czar role at the beginning of Trump's second term.The task force's vice chairs will be Emil Michael, Scott Kupor and Federal Trade Commission Chair Andrew Ferguson, while members will include Vice President JD Vance, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent and White House Chief of Staff Susie Wiles, according to the report. External advisers will also include Sacks and former Secretary of State Condoleezza Rice, the Journal said.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: US "Kicks Out" 2 Members Of Iranian Delegation For Overstaying
news.text: The United States has "kicked out" two members of the Iranian delegation who attended the recent UN General Assembly after they ignored an order to leave the country, the State Department said Saturday."Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in (New York) long after the United Nations General Assembly had passed. They have now been kicked out of the US," a US official told AFP, adding that Secretary of State Marco Rubio "means business."US media reported the State Department had told Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi and his delegation to leave the country Monday, and resorted to expelling the two members after learning from the Iranian mission to the UN they remained in the country on Friday.One member of the delegation left Friday night, while the second departed Saturday morning, according to Axios.US and Iranian officials had met the week prior in New York on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly.US President Donald Trump had rejected a proposal from Tehran to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, but told US media he expected talks to resume in the coming days.Iranian state news agency IRNA reported that Tehran had no more direct talks scheduled with Washington.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Trump touts ‘golden age’ at Ohio rally, urges voters to deliver GOP midterm wins
news.text: President Donald Trump swept into Ohio Saturday night promoting what he calls a new "golden age" for America, pointing to billions of dollars in investment and new jobs in the Buckeye State as he urged voters to help keep Republicans in power in November. For the third time in as many nights, Trump rallied supporters outside Dayton for Republicans Sen. Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, casting the midterms as a chance to extend the economic and political gains he said the GOP has delivered since his return to the White House. And with his own name absent from the ballot, Trump gave voters gathered a simple instruction. TRUMP CAMPAIGN INSIDER REVEALS STRATEGY BEHIND MIDTERM BLITZ THAT WHITE HOUSE HOPES PAYS OFF BIG "Just pretend that I’m running," Trump said. "When I run, we win." Trump, who carried Ohio in all three of his presidential campaigns, later echoed the same message as he sought to rally his political coalition behind Republicans fighting to maintain control of Congress. "If you don’t mind, please pretend that I’m on the ballot," Trump said. "And you need to turn out for a midterm victory." The president used much of the rally to make an economic case for the Republican ticket, declaring Ohio is "booming" as he hailed investments he credited to both his trade and tariff policies. Trump pointed to a $400 million Stellantis investment in Toledo and an $850 million Electra aerospace investment near Springfield. Weaving in an anecdote about his daily aspirin habit, the president also featured Bayer’s plans for a $2.2 billion pharmaceutical manufacturing campus near Columbus, which the company says will support approximately 600 permanent jobs and 1,500 construction jobs. "Your state is booming," Trump told the gathered crowd. "Every state is booming." FIRST DATA CENTER BILL CLEARS HOUSE AS BOTH PARTIES SCRAMBLE FOR ANSWERS ON AFFORDABILITY Trump credited the investments to his tariff agenda, arguing the U.S. is finally leveling the playing field after years of other countries using tariffs against American products while giving companies a powerful incentive to build at home. The president also threw his support behind Husted’s Ratepayer Protection Act, legislation aimed at shielding consumers from additional electricity costs associated with data centers. "We want them," Trump said of data centers. "There’s so much money to be made for Ohio. You can’t just turn them off. They’ll go to China." Husted brought the legislation to the Senate floor days before the rally, where it failed to advance. President Trump pledged to sign it if Congress can send it to his desk. TRUMP DEFENDS $5,000 DIVIDEND PROPOSAL, PRAISES 'BEAUTIFUL' TARIFFS ON 'INGRAHAM ANGLE' "I will sign this Ratepayer Protection Act into law immediately," Trump said. Trump broadened his victory lap from Ohio to the country as a whole, hailing stock market records, manufacturing growth, investment and employment while contrasting his own administration’s economic record with former President Joe Biden's. "Our nation is doing better now than ever before," Trump said. He also praised GOP-backed tax provisions, including no tax on tips and overtime, and reiterated his previously announced proposal for $5,000 payments to adult Americans if Republicans retain the House and Senate. Trump then shifted to immigration and Springfield, Ohio, dedicating his recitation of the poem "The Snake" to the city that became a national flashpoint during the 2024 presidential campaign over an influx of Haitian nationals into the community. "I dedicate this to Springfield, Ohio," Trump said. "They went through hell." After finishing the poem, which the president has long admired as an immigration allegory, he told the crowd, "That’s what happened at our border," before hailing his administration’s immigration crackdown. The president also briefly touched on Venezuela, claiming the U.S. had more than recouped the costs of its military operation against former Venezuelan dictator Nicolas Maduro through the country's vast oil resources. "We paid for the cost of the war many, many times over," Trump said. "We’re making a fortune with it." Trump repeatedly weaved the election 31 days away into his remarks, urging Ohioans to support Husted, Ramaswamy and Republican congressional candidates. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He also pitched Ohio as a potential home for the U.S. National Space Academy, citing both the state's aviation history and the Wright brothers. "If we win the midterms, Ohio will be very, very strongly considered for this," Trump said. "I really want you to go out and vote again for John Husted and for Vivek."
news.summary: President Donald Trump urged Ohio rally-goers to "pretend I'm on the ballot" as he stumped for Jon Husted and Vivek Ramaswamy in the midterms.

news.title: Cornell president vows transparency amid outrage over fraternity rape case  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
Cornell University’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, has called the alleged 2024 gang rape of a student at a fraternity house “deeply disturbing”, pledging greater transparency amid mounting outrage over how the school handled the case.

“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said in an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community on Saturday.

He characterised the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and said it would weigh on the university for years to come. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanisation and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use,” he said.

The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 and has sued the university and seven former students.

Scrutiny over Cornell’s handling of the case intensified after New York Governor Kathy Hochul said newly released information had undermined her confidence in the local prosecutor, who initially declined to bring charges.

Hochul subsequently appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to take over the criminal investigation, saying she would “not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug”.

The case has also renewed scrutiny of the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving victims who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs, even if they later became too intoxicated to consent.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten had cited the legal provision in defending his original decision not to pursue charges. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to it.

At a student assembly hearing on Thursday, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

In Saturday’s video, Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s handling of the case and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”.

James’s appointment has placed the case under a prosecutor whose office has repeatedly clashed with President Donald Trump. She has separately described the case as “an active criminal investigation”.

news.title: Trump Pledges $90 Medicare Premium Each To 20 Million Seniors
news.text: President Donald Trump is promising more payments to voters just ahead of the November 3 midterm elections - this time, to more than 20 million seniors, giving them $90 each to help pay for Medicare premiums.The announcement, made late Friday night by Trump on social media, comes after the president last month said about 1 million people would get rebate checks of $500 for Affordable Care Act premiums. He has also promised on the campaign trail to send every American adult $5,000 if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in the midterm elections.That pledge - which would require approval from Congress - would likely cost more than $1 trillion, adding to the deficit and worsening inflation.Polls show Americans increasingly blame Trump for the high cost of gasoline and groceries with just 17% approving of his handling of inflation. Trump has sought to shrug off concerns about affordability, saying the economy is booming.The White House said the $90 payments for seniors will come from the Medicare Improvement Fund, established by Congress in 2008 as flexible funding to improve program operations and payments to health care providers.Medicare Part B enrollees can expect to receive a one-time payment in October, either through direct deposit or by check, the White House said. Total monthly costs for the program - which covers costs like doctor's visits, ambulance services and lab tests - start around $200 and vary with income.To be eligible, seniors must be living in the US and not be already receiving premium assistance from Medicaid or paying adjusted monthly premiums based on income, according to the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services. Seniors enrolled in Medicare Advantage, a private plan alternative to traditional Medicare coverage, are not eligible for the payment. More than half of eligible Medicare beneficiaries have Medicare Advantage, according to healthcare research nonprofit KFF.Previous administrations have not used the Medicare Improvement Fund in this way, although Congress has periodically taken out money from the fund to pay for other priorities, said Larry Levitt, KFF's executive vice president for health policy. For example, $20.74 billion was used for the creation of the Affordable Care Act in 2010."The Medicare Improvement Fund language is quite broad and gives substantial discretion to the administration," Levitt said.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: That pledge - which would require approval from Congress - would likely cost more than $1 trillion, adding to the deficit and worsening inflation.

news.title: Ken Paxton’s estranged wife urges voters to back his Senate bid, yet avoids mentioning him by name
news.text: The estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton urged voters to stand behind the entire Republican midterm ticket in an ad released Saturday, though she neglected to name Paxton directly. Texas state Sen. Angela Paxton, who filed for divorce from Paxton last year citing “biblical grounds,” appeared in an ad telling Texans that she is “voting for the Republican ticket on Nov. 3,” but did not cite Paxton’s Senate bid by name. She did, however, invite voters to “talk about the elephant in the room.” “In a general election, it’s not as much about the individual players on the team; it’s about getting the whole team across the finish line,” Paxton said in the ad. “Either we hold every Republican seat, or we hand the future of Texas to the other team.” Angela Paxton’s office did not immediately respond to a request for comment on whether she plans to vote for her estranged husband herself. Ken Paxton’s tenure as attorney general has been beset by allegations of abuse of office and bribery. Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House of Representatives in 2023, but the state Senate later acquitted him. The Senate trial, however, touched on allegations of infidelity. Paxton has denied any wrongdoing. The ad comes as Paxton’s daughter, Mattie Hayworth, recently appeared in an ad for her father alongside her husband and children. Hayworth criticized “liberal politicians” as a graphic showing Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., alongside Paxton’s Democratic opponent, James Talarico, came over the screen. “When they come after you, my dad goes after them to bring down prices and stand up for families,” Hayworth said. As Election Day nears, Talarico holds a slight edge over Paxton, defying the deep-red profile of Texas, where Republicans haven’t lost a statewide race since 1994 and Democrats haven’t won a U.S. Senate seat since 1988. According to an NBC5 Dallas/Telemundo Station Group poll in late September, Talarico was at 46% and Paxton at 43%, within the survey’s margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The poll acknowledges another 8% of potential voters who are still undecided in the race. NBC News currently defines the race as a toss-up. The ad featuring Angela Paxton, which was funded by Texas PAC, a political action committee affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune, comes as the Texas Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the current cycle. President Donald Trump, who endorsed Paxton over incumbent Sen. John Cornyn in the Republican primary, has urged voters to get behind the state attorney general. His super PAC, MAGA Inc., has also put millions into Paxton’s race. The president has visited Texas twice in the last month — first for the GOP midterm convention in Dallas and then again this week for a rally in Denton, which comes as part of Trump’s 17-state campaign blitz. In a separate campaign appearance Friday night in Alabama, Trump reiterated the high stakes associated with Texas’ race. “Last night, I went to Texas, where we won by a lot, and then I went to Oklahoma, and they said, ‘Why is he going to Texas?’” Trump said. “Because we have to win that race. Ken Paxton has to win.”
news.summary: The estranged wife of Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton urged voters to stand behind the entire Republican midterm ticket in an ad released Saturday, though she neglected to name Paxton directly.
news.author: Kyla Guilfoil

news.title: Brazil election: Lula, Flavio Bolsonaro face off in tight race shaped by Trump factor
news.text:
ReutersBrazilians are preparing to vote in a tight election between President Lula and Flavio Bolsonaro on Sunday.

millions out of poverty, made a dramatic comeback to office in 2022 elections after a massive corruption scandal that saw him jailed for over 18 months.The charges, thrown out on procedural grounds, election, but he has not endorsed Flavio Bolsonaro.The US president has wielded tariffs and sanctions to pressure Brasilia over complaints ranging from the trial against his ally Jair Bolsonaro to alleged unfair trade practices.Lula has repeatedly warned him not to "meddle" in the elections.Flavio Bolsonaro's rallies have featured massive US flags and images of Trump.Buoyed by his father's legacy, he has been a formidable rival for Lula, even as it emerged he was under investigation for corruption over the financing of the biopic "Dark Horse" about his father.The younger Bolsonaro has vowed a hardline approach to crime and fiscal austerity amid rising public debt.Carlos Roberto dos Santos, 62, a cattle rancher in the southeastern city Barretos who supports Bolsonaro, told AFP he news.title: Iranian President says enemy failed to achieve economic war objectives
news.text: Digital Desk | New Delhi, Oct 4 (IANS) Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has said that the government has adopted a new arrangement to manage the “special conditions” facing the country, while asserting that efforts to pressure Iran economically have failed to achieve their intended objectives. Pezeshkian, in a post on X, said the country had been facing intensified economic pressure but maintained that the government, with the support of the Iranian people, had prevented the enemy from achieving its goals in what he described as an “economic war”. “The government has adopted a new arrangement to manage these special conditions. The enemy's plan in recent months has been to cut off the country's vital arteries with the aim of pressuring the noble people of Iran. Economic pressure has intensified, but by the grace of God, with the accompaniment of the people and the measures taken by our colleagues in the government, we have not allowed the enemy's objectives in the economic war to be realized,” the Iranian President posted. Pezeshkian's remarks came amid continuing tensions surrounding the conflict and mounting economic pressure on Iran. US President Donald Trump, meanwhile, said the war with Iran would end “very quickly” and predicted that oil prices would fall sharply once the conflict was over. He also portrayed Iran as facing severe military and economic pressure. Speaking to reporters after arriving in Texas and later during a visit to a Peterbilt Motors facility in Denton, Trump said Iran faced a choice over how the conflict would end. “Iran will very soon be ending one way or the other,” Trump told reporters. “It'll either just say, look, they have 301 per cent inflation. They have no money, they have no currency. Their military has been defeated, their navy is gone, their air force is gone, everything's gone.” “And, one way or the other, it's going to end very quickly. And when that ends, oil prices are going to drop like a rock,” he said.

news.title: Jon Gruden backs Republican Jon Husted in Senate race
news.text:
Former Las Vegas Raiders and Super Bowl-winning head coach Jon Gruden has given Republican Senate candidate Jon Husted his full support during a surprise visit at a campaign rally for President Donald Trump in Vandalia, Ohio.

Gruden, 63, a native of Sandusky, Ohio, who went to college at the University of Dayton, took the stage and began endorsing his former college football teammate.

“I want to thank everybody for growing up. Thank you guys, for being here. I love you guys,” Gruden said. “… Jon Husted is a lot more than my friend. He was a great player. He intercepted 17 passes on the gridiron.

“I know why he was a great player. It was because of his work ethic, and his commitment, and his native Dayton mental toughness. He will never quit on you or anybody. Let’s hear it for Husted.”

After the crowd gave Gruden a large round of applause, he had one last thing to tell them.

“Before you know it. This election is over, yes? It’s over,” Gruden said. “But what we gotta do is we gotta do our part. Early voting starts Tuesday. Can we be there or not?”

Gruden went on to tell the crowd to get their friends out and go vote.

“Husted back in action. Lets go. Thank you!” Gruden said.

In the past, Gruden has shown his support for President Trump, as the two were seen playing golf together in 2025, when Trump called him “A really nice guy.”

While Gruden isn’t known for being involved in politics, he was known for being the head coach of the Raiders.

His first stint happened between 1998-2001 and came to an end after he was traded to the Tampa Bay Buccaneers.

In 2002, Gruden’s Buccaneers met the Raiders in Super Bowl 37 and defeated them 48-21.

In 2008, Gruden was locked to remain with the Buccaneers until 2011, when he signed a three-year extension after starting the season with a 9-3 record. Tampa Bay ended up collapsing in the second half of the season in an ironic twist of fate, as they dropped their final game of the season to the Raiders.

Gruden went on to have a career as a broadcaster, serving as a color commentator on Monday Night Football.

In 2018, he came back to coaching after agreeing to join forces with the Raiders again.

Gruden’s second stint finished with a 22-31 record, and he would eventually resign from the job after an email scandal leaked of him using racist language, mocking an openly gay NFL player, and being unsupportive of the emergence of women in the NFL as officials.

news.title: A $28B hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban
news.text: In a commercial kitchen outside Raleigh, North Carolina, Nicholas Hohns spreads a blue-green goo into a gridded mold, making one of his company's signature products: potent THC gummies, featuring the primary intoxicating compound found in marijuana.It's a business he might soon have to give up. America's multibillion-dollar market for impairing hemp products — from THC seltzers sold at some Target stores to smokable cannabis flowers, and different from the regulated legal marijuana industry — faces potential elimination after Congress voted to close a loophole in federal law that has allowed it to flourish.Advocates for the industry, along with some lawmakers, are fighting to save it. The short-term government-funding bill signed by President Donald Trump last month delayed the effective date of the 'hemp THC ban' from Nov. 12 to Dec. 11, giving Congress more time to consider regulating the products rather than banning them.'It's such a weird spot to be in,' said Hohns. 'You worked 100 hours a week for the past four years, and, yeah, you made some money. But now you might have nothing to show for it.'Sen. Mitch McConnell closed a loophole in the hemp law he championedMarijuana and hemp are the same plant — cannabis. Marijuana is cultivated for high levels of THC in its flowers. Low-THC hemp has historically been grown for its sturdy fibers, food or wellness products. 'Rope, not dope' was long the motto of farmers who supported legalizing hemp.To give farmers a new cash crop, Kentucky Republican Sen. Mitch McConnell successfully pushed the legalization of industrial hemp in the 2018 farm bill.But the way that law defined hemp — as having less than 0.3% of a specific type of THC, called delta-9, by weight — opened a huge loophole. Beverages or snacks could meet that threshold and still contain more than enough THC to get people high.Vape oil, gummy candies, chips, sodas and other unregulated, untested products laden with hemp-derived THC spread around the country, including in gas stations or convenience stores, where they were available even to teens. Some businesses started selling marijuana under the theory that raw marijuana's THC is in a form called THC-A, which only turns into impairing delta-9 when heated or burned.The products evaded state prohibitions on recreational weed or undercut heavily taxed and regulated cannabis where it is legal.Dozens of states responded by regulating or banning impairing hemp products.McConnell finally closed the loophole late last year by inserting a hemp THC ban into a measure that ended the longest government shutdown in history.The ban, which limits the amount of THC in hemp products to 0.4 milligrams per container, wouldn't take effect for a year.An industry tries to save itselfThe ban 'threatens to reduce retail revenues by $28.3 billion, displacing 225,000 jobs and reducing state sales tax potential by $2.1 billion,' according to a report last month from Whitney Economics, which studies the market.The industry hopes to save itself by restricting impairing products to people 21 and older, limiting how much THC can be in a package, and banning imported cannabis compounds.The owners of Kentucky's Cornbread Hemp, Eric Zipperle and Jim Higdon, are prepared to cap their products at, say, 5 milligrams if that's what it takes to win support from lawmakers. But the 0.4 milligram limit would destroy their business, they said.'If it goes through in December, this place is toast — it's gone,' Zipperle said.They have 105 employees, sell hemp beverages in 18 states and expect to bring in $65 million this year.The 0.4-milligram cap is so low that it would ban even some non-impairing CBD products, such as topical lotions, said Jonathan Miller, general counsel of the industry group U.S. Hemp Roundtable.Some consider other workHohns, who runs Deutermann Farms in Clayton, North Carolina, entered the hemp industry after losing his job as a personal trainer during the COVID-19 pandemic. North Carolina has not legalized either medical or recreational marijuana, but many of the edibles Hohns makes are more potent than what's available in states that have.'When I started seeing THC edibles being sold … I was like, I got 18 months to two years to make money in this industry,' Hohns said. 'No way is the government just going to sit here and let us do this when this was supposed to be for fiber, plastics, building materials, rope.'That was more than four years ago. Hohns kept his capital investments minimal, fearing a shutdown. He has considered making other products, such as creatine gummies, if he has to get out of the hemp THC business.Things have been more stressful for others. Drinkin' Buds, a cannabis beverage company in Sheboygan, Wisconsin, has mothballed production. Co-founder Matt Swanson took himself off the payroll on Thursday.'There's just so much uncertainty,' Swanson said. 'I'm actively looking for employment.'Allies and opponents line upAmong those who have come to the defense of the hemp industry are alcohol retailers, including Total Wine & More. Sales of cannabis seltzers have helped offset falling alcohol sales.Opponents include people who say the products are dangerous.'I have sympathy for people losing their jobs, but I also have sympathy for the many, many more people whose lives are affected by this,' said Kevin Sabet, CEO of Smart Approaches to Marijuana.The regulated legal marijuana industry, which sees hemp THC as unfair competition, also supports the ban. Cory Harris, a lobbyist for state-legal cannabis operators, suggested that dire predictions about its effect on the intoxicating hemp industry are overstated.While the ban would end interstate sales of products like THC seltzers and gummies, some could find a home in legal in-state markets, he said. It's possible THC drinks could be sold at stores in the states where they were produced. States like North Carolina could adopt legal hemp programs.'If you go from having virtually no rules to suddenly having an awful lot of rules, that's a buzzkill,' Harris said. 'Welcome to our world. But if you establish your whole business within a legally questionable loophole, that's just sort of the risk you take.

news.title: Cornell president vows transparency amid outrage over fraternity rape case  | Barbados Gazette –
news.text:
Cornell University’s president, Michael Kotlikoff, has called the alleged 2024 gang rape of a student at a fraternity house “deeply disturbing”, pledging greater transparency amid mounting outrage over how the school handled the case.

“My heart aches when I think of what she experienced,” Kotlikoff said in an eight-minute video message to the Cornell community on Saturday.

He characterised the past week as one of the most difficult in the university’s history and said it would weigh on the university for years to come. “It raises heartbreaking and troubling issues about sexual assault, dehumanisation and aspects of party culture, alcohol and drug use,” he said.

The woman, identified in court documents as Jane Doe, alleges she was sexually assaulted by multiple members of the Chi Phi fraternity in 2024 and has sued the university and seven former students.

Scrutiny over Cornell’s handling of the case intensified after New York Governor Kathy Hochul said newly released information had undermined her confidence in the local prosecutor, who initially declined to bring charges.

Hochul subsequently appointed state Attorney General Letitia James as special prosecutor to take over the criminal investigation, saying she would “not allow anyone to sweep this case under the rug”.

The case has also renewed scrutiny of the “voluntary intoxication loophole” in New York law that makes it difficult to prosecute sexual assaults involving victims who voluntarily consumed alcohol or drugs, even if they later became too intoxicated to consent.

Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten had cited the legal provision in defending his original decision not to pursue charges. Hochul has pledged to push for changes to it.

At a student assembly hearing on Thursday, several speakers called for Kotlikoff’s resignation.

In Saturday’s video, Kotlikoff reaffirmed his support for an independent review of the university’s handling of the case and said Cornell’s Board of Trustees would announce details next week. He also called for a “serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life”.

James’s appointment has placed the case under a prosecutor whose office has repeatedly clashed with President Donald Trump. She has separately described the case as “an active criminal investigation”.
