news.title: USD 5,000 for Every American Adult? Donald Trump’s Midterm Pledge, Cost and What Polls Say
news.text:
US President Donald Trump has promised USD 5,000 to every American adult citizen if Republicans win control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, pitching the move as a choice between a personal cash windfall and economic ruin. In a Truth Social video posted on Saturday, Trump repeated a commitment he first made last month at the Republican National Committee's inaugural midterm convention in Dallas, saying, "If Republicans win the House of Representatives and the Senate, I'm going to give all adult citizens in the United States of America $5,000." He has branded the proposal the "Republican Dividend".

Trump also warned of dire consequences if Democrats prevail. "If the Democrats win, you will have an economic depression, much like 1929," he said, adding that Democratic policies would raise taxes and cause a "disaster". The video offered no economic analysis to back that forecast.

How Would The Payments Be Funded?

Trump estimated the Republican Dividend would cost roughly USD 1 trillion and said the government could afford it because tariffs were bringing in "massive amounts" of money. He also claimed that USD 21 trillion had been invested in the United States over the past 15 months. Investment commitments, however, are not a pool of federal cash available for direct payments. Donald Trump Predicts Short-Lived Iran Conflict, Says Situation ‘Working Out Very Well’.

The proposal makes no distinction between taxpayers and adults who owe no federal income tax. Nothing has been said on whether Congress must approve the spending, how tariff revenue would be allocated, or when any cheques could arrive.

What Do Polls Say About The Offer?

Recent surveys suggest the idea has some appeal, but few voters believe it will materialise. An Economist/YouGov poll found likely voters opposed the proposed cheques by 45 percent to 43 percent. Among all registered voters in the sample, 48 percent favoured sending USD 5,000 to every adult citizen, while 40 percent opposed it. Yet only 38 percent called it a good idea, against 45 percent who called it a bad one. Sixty-one percent said Trump probably or definitely would not deliver the payments if Republicans retained Congress, while 22 percent expected him to. The poll covered 1,461 registered voters from September 11 to 14, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3.3 percentage points. A separate Verasight survey looked at electoral impact. It found 33 percent were less likely to vote Republican because of the pledge, 15 percent were more likely, and 52 percent said it made no difference. Voters aged 18 to 29 split 41 percent less likely to 19 percent more likely, while independents split 31 percent to 12 percent in the same direction. Sixty-three percent of Republicans said the offer would not change their vote. The survey covered 1,500 US adults from September 16 to 21, with a margin of error of plus or minus 2.6 percentage points.

Other Payments Trump Has Floated

Trump cited the USD 1,776 "warrior dividend" paid to eligible service members in December 2025 as proof he can deliver. "Everybody got their money," he said. "I did it, and I do it again."

The idea has shifted form several times. The DOGE Dividend surfaced in February 2025, when Azoria CEO James Fishback proposed returning 20 percent of savings generated by the Department of Government Efficiency. Trump and Elon Musk backed the concept of USD 5,000 payments to taxpayers, but it never moved beyond a proposal. A tariff dividend then appeared later that year as a possible USD 2,000 rebate for working-class families, before evolving into the current USD 5,000 midterm pledge.

This week, Trump also said checks of "nearly $100" would go to millions of seniors to help cover Medicare Part B premiums, and suggested residents near data centres could receive a dividend. A targeted USD 500 Affordable Care Act premium rebate is already being distributed. No payments under the USD 5,000 plan have been approved, funded or sent.

news.title: Michael Goodwin: Trump faces an uphill battle to sell voters on his agenda before the midterms — here’s how he can do it
news.text:
Although he wrote and has lived his life by the “Art of the Deal,” Donald Trump faces a giant hurdle in trying to persuade voters to keep his party in control of Washington.

Over the next month, he must successfully sell the idea that his presidency has been a big success, and that he needs a Republican congress to help him finish the job.

Midterm elections commonly spell trouble for the occupant of the White House, but Trump’s challenge is far from ordinary.

With his personal popularity sagging and his party a decided underdog in swing districts and states, the president must move mountains of voters and do it quickly.

Election Day on Nov. 3 is approaching on the fast track, and the urgency is compounded because nearly all states allow some form of early voting.

Showing that he realizes his political life and legacy are on the line, the president plans to spend most of October barnstorming America, with reports saying he aims to visit at least 10 states.

The scale of the challenge is indicated by the fact that his first stops were in Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama — states that are usually reliably red, but are not yet secured this year.

The extended tour is unusual, but Trump has little choice. With polls and betting markets predicting Dems will win majorities in both the House and Senate, the president’s final two years in office will be the stuff of nightmares unless he can engineer a stunning comeback.

Otherwise, we know what the template of failure looks like — the second half of his first term. After Dems won a House majority in 2018 and made Nancy Pelosi Speaker, she orchestrated investigations of nearly every breath the president took and every dollar he spent.

Thanks to the help of leftist partisans carrying media credentials and a corrupt deep state, she turned the Russia-gate hoax into an impeachment farce.

A similar fate would be certain to befall the president again, with Dems now largely running on a “Get Trump” platform. Under the sway of burn-it-down radicals, their agenda ranges from more impeachment to imposing sky-high taxes on families and businesses, demonizing Israel and re-opening borders to all comers.

Trump knows as much, but his schedule shows he believes voters can be persuaded that he and the GOP congress have earned the right to stay the course.

In important ways, the president has a strong case, but the success of his travels and rallies will depend on how persuasively he makes that case.

Messaging trap

With the Real Clear Politics average of polls showing he has an approval rating of just 38%, compared with 60% disapproval, he faces a steep climb.

Inflation is still driving up prices, and most Americans are giving Trump poor grades on the economy. Majorities are also tired of the war in Iran, so how the president makes his final pitch could be the deciding factor in November.

One hurdle is that he has fallen into the trap of telling people how great everything is when their day-to-day experiences, especially when it comes to rising prices, are telling them something very different.

The message that all is well was a bust when Joe Biden and Kamala Harris tried it in 2024, and it’s not working any better for Trump.

One factor is the president’s habit of premature declarations of victory, over both inflation and Iran. An alternative approach, even at this late hour, would be to acknowledge public concerns and explain why he believes he and a GOP congress will achieve widely beneficial victories.

To judge from comments he made at the White House on Thursday, the president is not yet ready to go there.

“I give us an A+ on the government, on economics, on everything” he said, according to Politico. An AP-NORC poll found just 26% approve of his handling of the economy, with a mere 17% happy with how he has managed the cost of living.

More alarming, a whopping 65% told pollsters White House policies are contributing to price hikes on everyday goods.

Countering that sentiment is difficult, but it is essential to highlight economic success stories. The Census Bureau reports that median household income is the highest on record at $87,400.

Working class key

Similarly, The Wall Street Journal reports that the 4.2% unemployment rate is “at a historically low level that indicates the labor market remains generally healthy.”

Stock markets have soared as many businesses have reported record earnings, with the S&P 500 gaining 37% since Trump’s reelection.

Weaving these accomplishments together while also recognizing that many families feel left out is difficult, but the effort is essential. Charting when and why the tide will change and lift all boats would give voters concrete reasons to stick with the team in place.

Railing against the polls as being biased won’t work, nor will boasts that the nation is living in a golden age of peace and prosperity.

Ditto for promoting grand Washington construction projects, whether it be an expanded White House ballroom or an Arch of Triumph armed with snipers and drones.

They are not likely to win over disillusioned voters, especially those troubled by Trump family members taking financial advantage of the presidency.

As for Iran, many Americans no doubt forget his patient efforts to negotiate a treaty for the mullahs to voluntarily give up their nuclear weapons project.

The regime’s refusal to even consider the idea led to the US and Israeli attacks that, I continue to believe, were fully justified.

Also absent so far in the president’s election-year pitch is the working-class appeal that lifted him to a smashing victory over Harris two years ago.

Those appeals were the heart of his campaign, just as they were in his shocking upset win over Hillary Clinton in 2016.

Two October events in the ’24 race still stand out as hilarious and wildly effective. In the first, Trump spent 30 minutes working in a McDonald’s outside Philadelphia. He wore a store apron over his suit and learned how to prepare french fries and handed bags of them to cars from a drive-through window.

Ten days later, in Green Bay, Wis., he got off his plane and climbed into the passenger seat of a large garbage truck that featured his name.

Sporting a yellow and orange safety vest over a white shirt, Trump asked reporters, “How do you like my garbage truck?”

It came just one day after Biden had said something to the effect that all Trump supporters were garbage.

Point made!

Both events were hailed because they were funny, as well as consistent with his pitch to working-class Americans.

It’s not a coincidence that he carried both Wisconsin and Pennsylvania that November, along with five other swing states.

His challenge now is to help his party do it all again.
news.summary: Midterm elections commonly spell trouble for the occupant of the White House, but President Trump’s challenge is far from ordinary.

news.title: Trump stresses importance of good relations with leaders of nuclear powers
news.text:
WASHINGTON, October 4. /TASS/. US President Donald Trump stressed the importance of good relations with leaders of nuclear powers.

"[Chinese] President Xi [Jinping] just left," Trump said at a rally in Ohio on Saturday, referring to the Chinese leader’s state visit to the United States on September 23-25. The US president said he had previously been asked "Why is he being nice to President Xi?" "Isn't it nice to get along with the leaders of massive nations, massive nuclear nations? Isn't it nice to have a good relationship?" Trump said.

The US president also said: "We get along great. I get along great with [North Korean leader] Kim Jong Un, okay?" He added, "But here's the difference: Iran will never have a nuclear missile." The Iranian authorities have repeatedly said they do not seek to acquire nuclear weapons.

The rally focused on the US midterm congressional elections scheduled for November 3. Voters will elect 33 of the 100 members of the Senate and all 435 members of the House of Representatives.

news.title: Trump Uses Crude Remark While Predicting Ohio GOP Ticket Wins
news.text: President Donald Trump used a crude remark while urging supporters to turn out for November's midterm elections, telling a rally crowd Saturday that Republicans would "shove it up their ass" if they score major victories at the ballot box. "Just get out and vote. If you do that, we're going to win, and we're going to win big! And we're going to shove it up their ass, ok?" Trump said while promoting Ohio's Republican ticket. The comment drew cheers from supporters and came as Trump ramps up campaigning ahead of the November 3 midterms, with control of Congress at stake and Democrats showing signs of momentum in several competitive races. The president has increasingly used blunt and confrontational language on the campaign trail as he seeks to energize Republican voters and boost turnout. Trump's remarks came during an appearance at Butler High School in Vandalia backing Ohio Republicans, including Senate candidate Jon Husted and gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy, as the party seeks to hold one of the nation's most closely watched Senate seats. Silence on Data Centers The profane line drew one of the loudest reactions of the event, but the crowd was noticeably quieter later when Trump made the case for data centers and artificial intelligence infrastructure. Trump argued that expanding data-center capacity would help strengthen the economy and preserve America's technological edge, particularly against China. The muted response stood out during a speech otherwise punctuated by applause lines and attacks on Democrats. Trump also warned that a Democratic victory would trigger a "1929-style economic depression." "If the Republicans win, you will each have $5,000 in your pocket," Trump said. Trump appeared to be referring to his proposed "Trump Dividend," a plan unveiled in September that would provide $5,000 payments to adult U.S. citizens if Republicans retain control of Congress. Trump later returned to familiar arguments about reducing the size of government, claiming federal agencies employ too many unnecessary workers. 'Pretend I'm Running' Beyond his economic message, Trump repeatedly framed the midterm elections as a referendum on his presidency. "I'm asking you to just pretend I'm running, because if we do, we're gonna win big," Trump told supporters. The comment underscored Trump's continued dominance over the Republican Party and his central role in GOP campaign efforts heading into the Nov. 3 elections. Trump urged supporters to focus on turnout, arguing that Republican victories in Ohio and across the country depended on voters showing up regardless of their feelings about individual candidates. "Even if you hate Jon Husted, even if you hate Vivek Ramaswamy, you're gonna go out, you're gonna vote," Trump said. Throughout the speech, Trump repeatedly suggested that next month's contests were as much about his political agenda as the Republican candidates on the ballot, casting the election as a test of his presidency and warning that Democratic gains would derail his plans. Springfield and immigration Later in the rally, Trump returned to one of his signature immigration themes and asked supporters whether they wanted to hear "The Snake," a spoken-word routine he has frequently performed at rallies. "Would anybody like to hear The Snake? We gotta whip it out," Trump said. Trump then referenced Springfield, Ohio, calling it "a quaint little town of 32,000" people and claiming it had taken in 35,000 migrants. However, Census Bureau estimates place Springfield's population at roughly 58,000. Recent reporting estimates the city's Haitian community at about 12,000 to 15,000 people, well below the figure Trump cited. "It didn't work out too well," Trump said. "They're being removed." The remarks prompted chants of "De-port! De-port!" from the audience. Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here.
news.summary: Trump used a crude remark while urging supporters to turn out and back Ohio Republicans in the midterm elections.

news.title: Pakistan’s Russian dilemma
news.text:
IT is difficult to imagine a single small gesture reducing decades-old hostility between two archrivals. Yet, such a moment was witnessed recently when Alok Dimri, India’s national coordinator for the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, visited Islamabad for a meeting. Talking to the state media, he said he was happy to be in Pakistan. It was a simple statement, but perhaps one that may ease some of the cross-border bitterness. 

Mr Dimri said this while visiting the National Council of Arts in Islamabad. The heritage, art, and culture that Pakistan and India share have repeatedly fallen victim to toxic narratives designed to provoke hate. Yet the cultural link carries a powerful sense of mutual belonging. It may be premature to read too much into the Indian delegate’s visit or to view his words as evidence of a thaw after last May’s stand-off. Still, the episode offers some hope: if leaders on both sides choose to move forward, the dialogue could quickly regain momentum.

However, optimism should be tempered — as should any expectation that Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will arrive in Islamabad to attend the SCO summit. If he did, it would be a miracle, and the biggest surprise in decades — even bigger than Rajiv Gandhi’s visit to Islamabad in 1988 to attend the Saarc summit or Atal Bihari Vajpayee’s arrival in Lahore in 1999. Both occasions had generated enormous hope for peace between the two neighbours. What actually followed is a familiar story.

Another miracle would be if Russian President Vladimir Putin attended the Islamabad SCO summit next year. Pakistan is more curious about this visit and hopes it may trigger a major shift in its geopolitics and ambitions in Central Asia, while influencing the regional discourse in ways that would irritate India. Pakistan would be keen to enhance its defence cooperation with Russia, but particularly interested in making some progress on the much-discussed railway from Moscow to Islamabad and establishing a freight corridor using existing 7,000-kilometre-long railway networks, with Pakistan linked to Russia through Central Asia and/or Iran. Over the decades, Pakistan, the Central Asian states, and Iran have conceived many transnational projects, and each time with great enthusiasm, yet none has materialised. Afghanistan is always made to bear the burden of the blame because of its complex relationship with Pakistan.

 Russia is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan.

Is it not interesting that the conventional wars fought by India and Pakistan collectively may not have lasted for more than a few weeks, and that Pakistan fought its longest war against the Soviet Union in Afghanistan? Pakistan and the Afghan mujahideen, together with the US, defeated the Russians, which was followed by the dismantling of the Soviet state. The Pakistani leadership still takes pride in that success.

Of course, times have changed, and Pakistan is looking to cultivate new economic and defence opportunities. Russia, however, is likely to remain cautious about deepening its cooperation with Pakistan. This is not because of their bitter past, from which both sides have moved on, but because of divergent regional interests, particularly over Afghanistan, and Russia’s deep and long-standing engagement with India.

Russian-Indian defence and economic cooperation is not necessarily an obstacle to developing ties with Pakistan. But it does mean that Islamabad cannot be regarded as a preferred partner in that context. The disparity in economic relations is significant: Pakistan’s bilateral trade with Russia is less than half a billion dollars, compared with around $69bn in India-Russia trade. The gap is even more pronounced in defence cooperation. India maintains a high level of military engagement with Russia through multiple military-technical cooperation frameworks, including joint research and development, co-development, co-production, and after-sales support. By contrast, Russia’s defence engagement with Pakistan remains selective and falls well short of a strategic military partnership.

At the same time, India’s diversification of its defence partnerships has not significantly weakened its relationship with Russia. Moscow may have reservations about some aspects of New Delhi’s growing defence ties with other countries, but there are no clear signs of a fundamental deterioration in bilateral relations. Russia’s interest in Pakistan is, therefore, largely geopolitical — maintaining engagement with Islamabad allows Moscow to show that its international network of partnerships is broad, while also keeping channels open with Pakistan’s political and security leaders, including those who have close ties with US President Donald Trump.

Public diplomacy is a domain through which Russia keeps its support club intact and seeks to enhance it, engaging Pakistani media, academics, opinion-makers, and policymakers through exchange programmes. The SCO is another platform Russia uses more extensively than other partners for public diplomacy.

Russia and Pakistan share counterterrorism concerns, but their approaches to Afghanistan differ sharply. Russia has recognised the Taliban regime, but Pakistan is fighting a tough war against terrorism and sees Afghanistan as a source of the war. In geo-economic terms, they have different priorities. Russia wants Afgha-n-istan in the camp of its Central Asian allies. At the same time, Pakistan is a major partner of the US in areas where the interests of the two countries converge in Afghanistan. This irritates not only Russia but also China, which wants the US to stay out of the region in its immediate neighbourhood. The US took two decades to leave Afghanistan, and China does not want to see it coming back.

It is not surprising that Indian-Russian relations have had few hiccups over decades. At the same time, Pakistan chose the US as its strategic partner after independence. Still, their relationship has not been smooth. Pakistan’s strategic partnership with China has also been tested recently, triggered by CPEC-related disputes and internal security concerns regarding Chinese nationals in Pakistan.

Perhaps Russia is a new love interest for a segment of Pakistan’s power elite, but the two have little to share. And the last optimistic note: what if India and Pakistan decide to live in peace? What would the geopolitical impact be? 

The writer is a security analyst.

news.title: Becerra’s battles are against Trump, who’s not on ballot
news.text:
Xavier Becerra walked into CNN’s Burbank studio Wednesday night as the heavy favorite to be California’s next governor. He walked out the same way. But anyone expecting the debate to demonstrate why the state’s former attorney general and Biden Cabinet secretary holds such a commanding lead in the race was disappointed.

For 60 minutes, the Democratic Party nominee, and Steve Hilton, his Republican challenger, seemingly fought to a draw in a race in which Becerra has been cruising.

Becerra’s campaign has kept him on a short leash for months, rationing public appearances and agreeing to exactly one general-election debate. Hilton opened the night’s stage by welcoming him to the campaign and thanking CNN “for bringing Xavier out of hiding.”

Given that the expectations for the well-seasoned but lackluster former state attorney general and Biden administration Health and Human Services secretary were low, Becerra cleared them comfortably. Becerra was sharper, quicker, and more articulate than many observers expected, and at times genuinely combative.

One word, 40 times

Becerra’s game plan was simple and predictable. By CNN’s count he said Donald Trump’s name at least 40 times in an hour – and wasn’t shy about tying Hilton to the president.

“He’s your supporter – you chased his endorsement,” Becerra asserted.

Asked about Hilton’s plan to eliminate state income taxes for middle-class Californians, Becerra answered: “You’re going to end up with Trump results if you follow Steve Hilton’s plans.”

Asked about artificial intelligence, Becerra went to the same well: “If you listen closely, you can hear Donald Trump in that response by Steve Hilton.”

On oil drilling, on homelessness, on immigration, on housing, the answer kept circling back to a man who is dominating national political headlines but has rarely campaigned in California and will not be on the California ballot in November.

It’s a predictable tactic in a state where the president is deeply unpopular, but it’s not a governing agenda and some 20 minutes into the debate, Hilton said what many viewers may have been thinking.

“All you ever say is Trump, Trump, Trump, and that’s nothing but an insult to every Californian,” the former Fox News host remarked.

The night’s sharpest contrast came on the issue of employment.

“Who’s been in charge when all those jobs have gone?” Hilton asked, referring to the state’s flagging film industry.

“Donald Trump,” Becerra replied.

“The Democrats,” Hilton shot back.

Both men were sticking to their scripts. Becerra wants voters thinking about Washington. Hilton wants them thinking about Sacramento, where Democrats have held every lever of power for 16 years.

The fourth man on the stage

Trump wasn’t the only absent figure who loomed large in the Burbank studio. Gavin Newsom, term-limited and leaving office in January – and presumably running for president in 2028 – also figured prominently. Becerra spent the night running against the man in the White House while Hilton spent it running against the man in the governor’s office – and against the record Becerra is asking voters to extend.

That’s an awkward spot for Becerra. He was attorney general for the first two years of Newsom’s tenure, and much of what Hilton pressed him on, from affordability and fraud to billions spent vainly on homelessness, is a record the two Democrats share. Every time Becerra pointed to Washington, Hilton pointed back to Sacramento and the governor whose job Becerra wants. Becerra was happy to keep the fight on Trump. He showed little appetite for a fight over Newsom’s record.

Hilton’s hits

When Becerra attacked Hilton’s proposed tax cuts with the old saw that the “definition of insanity” was doing the same thing over and over again and expecting different results, Hilton snapped back: “Like voting Democrat.”

It was an easy opening, and Becerra handed it to him. Hilton then used Becerra’s “insanity” line against him repeatedly. On the issue of whether California has over-regulated everything from business regulations to housing construction, Hilton used it to bash the Democratic supermajority control of Sacramento.

“The definition of insanity is believing that the people who put the red tape in place are somehow going to cut it,” he argued.

Hilton also pressed Becerra with specific questions about his record. When Becerra promised he would “cut red tape” to get more housing built, Hilton challenged him to name a time he had actually done so. The best he offered was his 2019 lawsuit against Huntington Beach for failing to meet state housing requirements, which is enforcing a mandate, not cutting regulations.

On affordability, the issue voters rank first, Hilton was crisp and consistent.

“The quickest way to get more money in people’s pockets is for the government to take less out,” he said.

On housing: “The quickest way to reduce the cost of housing is for the government to stop making it more expensive,” he added.

One can quarrel with the numbers, as Becerra did, arguing Hilton’s tax cuts would mostly help the wealthy and that Hilton’s “math doesn’t add up.” Hilton has said he’d pay for them by cutting high-speed rail, homelessness nonprofits, and 5% from all state departments’ budgets.

Hilton, whose lack of a necktie didn’t diminish his British accent, seems an unlikely populist. But he landed several punches while highlighting Becerra’s role as the Democratic establishment’s default choice.

“Xavier Becerra, you’re the candidate who is supported by the machine in Sacramento – the unions, big business, all these people that, for 16 years, have given us the highest cost of living in the country, made it impossible to build anything, given us the highest unemployment rate, the highest poverty rate.”

Becerra’s best moment

The son of Mexican immigrants, Becerra went after Hilton over federal enforcement raids, which are unpopular in California: “Steve thinks it’s perfect to let ICE mercenaries come on into California, and he welcomes it.”

Hilton responded by criticizing Becerra’s own record at HHS, where the department lost track of thousands of migrant children who had crossed the border alone.

“And you stand here lecturing people about immigration when you treated these most vulnerable children, unaccompanied children, in this way,” Hilton lectured.

He also reminded viewers that, as HHS secretary, Becerra kept a mask mandate in place for 2- and 3-year-olds in Head Start programs. Becerra’s half-hearted response was that he was following the medical experts’ advice at the time and that allowing “politicians” to dictate health policy is a fraught approach.

Becerra was at his most likable defending Hollywood. “We’ve got to keep Hollywood in Hollywood,” he said. “We don’t want it to be in Sydney, Australia. It shouldn’t be SydneyWood.”

Where Hilton came up short

As the underdog, Hilton had to make the most of a debate that will likely be the first and the last less than five weeks before Election Day. Yet, he was flatter than usual for stretches and neglected to highlight some of his interesting policy proposals and campaign promises, including lowering gas prices to $3 a gallon, eliminating taxes for people making less than $150,000, and cutting utility bills in half.

Hilton, who has spent the past year touring all 58 California counties, including Latino-majority cities most Republicans skip, also failed to press Becerra on the question that gave Kamala Harris the most trouble in her failed 2024 presidential campaign: What’s one thing you would do different than your predecessor?

Some of his swings landed hard. He read out former Obama and Biden adviser Susan Rice’s reported description of Becerra as an “idiot” and a “bitch-ass.” Becerra had no real response, simply waving it off: “Since when do I have to respond to politicians?”

That’s an incongruous line from a man who has been a career politician for 30 years, and it left Rice’s harsh verdict sitting there unanswered.

Yet, Hilton seemed surprised by some of the questions. He wandered into the weeds on vaccines, saying he supports vaccines but wants more parental discretion. That’s a defensible, nuanced position, but it’s not the type of punchy one-liner that rallies conservative base voters and wins over independents.

His housing pitch, built around counties bidding to host brand-new communities, is a bold idea that sounds great in a policy paper, but is difficult to convey in a 60-second answer.

Hilton is at his best when he keeps it simple: Costs are too high, Sacramento made them that way, and the people who did it are asking for four more years.

In the end, Hilton never fully shook the Trump label Becerra spent the night stitching onto him. He has said on the trail that “you can be anti-Trump and still vote for me.” He needed to explain why on Wednesday.

Where Becerra faltered

The low blow of the night was Becerra’s. Cornered on immigration, he turned personal and racial, telling Hilton, who emigrated from England: “You seem to welcome immigrants who look like you, but deport immigrants who look like me.” The suggestion that Hilton only wants white legal immigrants was a cheap shot, and Hilton chided his opponent for the racially divisive play.

“What a disgraceful remark that was,” he responded.

The AI exchange went little better. Hilton questioned whether Becerra could be trusted to regulate the industry, asking how much his campaign had taken in campaign contributions from OpenAI and Anthropic. Instead of answering, Becerra rattled off a list of other tech companies he had sued – Meta, Amazon, and Google – which was not the question.

Homelessness produced the night’s biggest surprise. Becerra promised to clear every homeless encampment in the state, a tougher line than any prominent California Democrat has taken. But he offered no specific plan for actually reducing homelessness. He promised to keep up “investments” in homeless services while focusing on addiction and mental illness, which is the same prescription Newsom has been writing for years.

Becerra never explained why that approach would work now. California has spent more than $24 billion on homelessness under Newsom, the problem has barely budged, and the spending has produced some egregious cases of fraud. Hilton cornered him on it, reminding viewers that during the spring primary debates Becerra gave Newsom an “A for effort” on homelessness. Few Californians who step over tents on their way to work would grade it that way.

Becerra never offered anything that sounded like a new idea or an original thought. His campaign refrain, that he is “not running on inflated promises,” is a nice line for a frontrunner, but hardly aspirational. Nearly every answer became another attack on Trump, which is not an answer to California’s problems.

There was some talk about housing, health insurance, and AI in state government. There was no big picture of what California looks like in 2030 under a Becerra administration, or why it would look different from the last 16 years.

One notable moment of agreement: both men oppose the billionaire wealth tax on the November ballot, even though most California Democrats support it.

Will it change anything?

Let’s be honest about the electoral math and the possible impact of one debate. Becerra led 60% to 38% in the latest mid-September Public Policy Institute of California poll, and 58% to 33% in the UC Berkeley IGS late August poll. Mail ballots start landing within days. Partly because Becerra has run a sleepy campaign, voters are mostly tuned out, and this debate did little to draw them in for the final weeks.

Still, despite Becerra’s lead, Hilton is asking the right questions, tapping into a high level of deep dissatisfaction Californians are feeling as costs continue to rise along with distrust in basic government competence. In the latest PPI survey a majority of likely California voters said the state is headed in the wrong direction.

Hilton’s best moments came when he asked the simple question: If you’re unhappy with how California is going, why keep voting for the people who got you here?

Becerra never answered it. Given the huge advantage Democrats enjoy in California, he was banking on the likelihood that doesn’t have to.
news.summary: In debate, Dem who wants to be governor complained about president 40 times

news.title: Yemen offensive
news.text:
IT appears that escalation is on the cards where the Houthi-Saudi and US-Iran conflicts are concerned. As per reports, Riyadh is planning an offensive to help the Yemeni government — which it backs — retake the strategically important Red Sea coast area from the pro-Iran Houthis, who captured it during a lightning offensive last month. Hostilities are continuing; there were reports on Saturday of both Riyadh and Sana’a being attacked. Meanwhile, members of the Makkah Joint Defence Agreement are due to hold an emergency meeting to discuss the Yemen situation. Regarding Iran, the US has reportedly ordered thousands more troops, as well as an aircraft carrier group, to the Gulf. This mirrors the build-up of American forces around Iran before the US-Israeli assault targeted the Islamic Republic in late February. Top US officials have reportedly met at Camp David to discuss the Yemen and Iran files.

Diplomacy, it seems, is giving way to more war in the Gulf and the wider Middle East. The humanitarian situation in Yemen is dire, with hundreds of thousands of people uprooted, while the UN says millions of Yemenis, including more than 2m infants, face acute hunger. If the Yemen war sucks in more regional states, it will complicate matters further. The best option, therefore, is for Muslim and Arab states to help restore the Saudi-Houthi ceasefire. The Houthi Ansarallah group must pledge to stop its attacks on Saudi Arabia, while ensuring free passage through Bab al-Mandeb. The Saudis, on their part, should consider lifting the blockade of Houthi territory, while encouraging all Yemeni factions to peacefully resolve the internal conflict. The Yemen war has been raging for over a decade, and previous external interventions have failed to end it; in fact, continued violence has exacerbated the humanitarian situation.

With regard to Iran, it appears that President Donald Trump’s administration has halted kinetic action only till the November US midterms, and plans to restart hostilities after elections are out of the way. This would be a grave error. US-Israeli aggression has caused great loss of life in Iran as well as damage to infrastructure, while the global economy has been shell-shocked due to the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. The world — particularly the states of the region — cannot afford more disruption and war. Mr Trump has turned down the recent Iranian proposal to open Hormuz. He should reconsider his strategy and restart dialogue with Tehran, while the Iranians should promise to reopen the strait if the US lifts its blockade of Iran and eases sanctions. The US leader has hailed the exit of American troops from Iraq. He should work on a similar plan to bring his forces home from elsewhere in the Gulf and end the Iran war.

news.title: Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election  - St. Vincent Tribune – Daily St
news.text:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro have wrapped up their election campaigns, each voicing confidence in victory ahead of Sunday’s tightly contested first-round presidential vote.

Lula, 80, closed his re-election bid on Saturday with a march through Sao Paulo, Brazil’s economic powerhouse, drawing what his campaign called a record crowd for a closing rally.

“Tomorrow, we’re going to win the elections in the first round,” he told supporters, describing Sunday’s vote as a choice between “democracy and barbarism” and promising to “defeat the far right”.

He has also framed the election as a test of Brazil’s sovereignty, warning against “meddling” by Washington.

Bolsonaro led a motorcycle caravan through towns in Sao Paulo state, echoing the campaign style of his father, before rallying later in Rio de Janeiro. “I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round,” he said.

The 45-year-old is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The former leader, 71, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.

The younger Bolsonaro was photographed at his rally holding a portrait of his father.

Trump has not formally endorsed Bolsonaro but has said he is watching the election “very closely”, a level of US interest that has become a flashpoint in the campaign.

Lula’s supporters have seized on it as evidence Washington is trying to meddle in the elections, while some Bolsonaro supporters, frustrated by the cost of living, say they would welcome US pressure if it helped force change at home.

Polls released on Saturday suggested Lula was still ahead but his lead was narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Such a result would send the race to a run-off on October 25 between the two frontrunners, a contest polls suggest would also be close.

It is a far tighter race than Lula’s last victory in 2022, when he beat the elder Bolsonaro by less than two percentage points.

news.title: Trump defends data centers in Ohio as he rallies to boost Jon Husted in a tight Senate race
news.text: President Donald Trump on Saturday defended data centers that power artificial intelligence projects but have become a contentious campaign issue nationwide, as he took his midterm tour to Ohio to insist his party will keep their majorities in Congress despite steep political headwinds.Trump took several minutes during his campaign rally in southwestern Ohio to promote his administration's action on data centers, saying he was seeking to ensure they "benefit local communities" and praised Republican Sen. Jon Husted for an ill-fated attempt this week to push forward legislation on the issue."Look, there's so much money to be made for Ohio. You can't just turn them off. They'll go to China," Trump said, repeating his defense of data centers that he had made before. The crowd, which had reacted enthusiastically as the president talked about other policies, was far more muted during the data centers remark.Trump is embarking on what he says will be a 32-day blitz ahead of the Nov. 3 elections, hitting the deep red states of Texas, Oklahoma and Alabama this week before pivoting to Ohio, a battleground state that's home to one of the top-tier Senate races this cycle.RELATED STORY | Trump and Vance hit the campaign trail in deep-red areas where GOP candidates seek a boostHusted — who was appointed to fill the Senate vacancy left by now-Vice President JD Vance — is running to win the seat outright. There is likely no path to a Senate majority for Democrats without flipping Ohio, where former three-term Sen. Sherrod Brown is trying to return to the Senate after losing to Republican Bernie Moreno two years ago.Since last year, Democrats have listed Ohio, along with states such as North Carolina and Maine, as key races to win control of the Senate. And this week, the head of the Senate GOP's campaign arm said Ohio is among 10 battleground races that are "within striking distance.""The good news for us is that Jon Husted is a closer," Sen. Tim Scott, the chairman of the National Republican Senatorial Committee, told reporters. "We're seeing the gap that was there between the two candidates, which was just a few points, now it is right at a dead-even race. So this is as tight as ticks, as we say in South Carolina."Data centers are a hot issue in the Ohio raceAt his rallies, Trump has been trying to convince voters that the economy is better than they feel it is, even though polls show Americans are frustrated with the way he's handled it. The high cost of living, including gas prices elevated by Trump's war on Iran, is a top issue in the Dayton area, too. And just days before Trump's rally, nearly 1,400 people were laid off from a truck factory in nearby Springfield.Trump's rally comes as Republicans worry that Husted's campaign has failed to adequately catch fire with voters in the Republican-dominated state. Brown and allied groups have hammered Husted for his role in attracting data centers to the state when he was lieutenant governor, and the NRSC has pinpointed it as a political vulnerability.The massive warehouse campuses powering artificial intelligence projects have become a toxic political issue, drawing bipartisan opposition in races across the country, with voters concerned about their impact on electricity prices, farmland and water supplies.The GOP-controlled Senate tried to advance legislation this week sponsored by Husted that would ask utility regulators to effectively charge large power users more, as consumers struggle with high energy costs. But it was blocked by nearly all Democrats."You got to remember, Sherrod Brown was for data centers, and Jon Husted is for data centers being responsible," Scott told reporters this week. "If a community doesn't want them, he doesn't want them either."But Trump has become one of data centers' most vocal proponents, shrugging aside voter concerns and arguing that the U.S. cannot cede advancements in AI to China."Senator Jon Husted gave billions in tax breaks to Big Tech to make sure they would build their data centers in Ohio," Brown wrote on X on Friday, ahead of Trump's visit. "Now, he's making Ohioans foot the bill."Brown's campaign also has hammered Husted for donations he's received from retail magnate Les Wexner, who once employed the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Husted has donated remaining Wexner contributions to an anti-human trafficking charity.There were several Epstein-themed signs outside the Vandalia school where the rally was being held, as more than a hundred protesters lined the road with a slew of anti-Trump and anti-Husted signs.But inside the school's gymnasium, the boisterous crowd — decked out in red "Make America Great Again" hats and "Trump 47" jerseys — greeted each Republican candidate enthusiastically as they awaited the president's arrival.RELATED STORY | New midterm polling gives Democrats an edge in battleground statesFrom the stage, Husted said the state had been through "hard times," noting his dad had worked at a factory that closed down. But he said Republicans in the state had turned it around."We now have the most jobs and the lowest unemployment rate we've ever had in the history of Ohio," he said.Meanwhile, in the governor's race, Republican Vivek Ramaswamy faces Democrat Dr. Amy Acton, the state's former COVID-era health director.A wealthy biotech entrepreneur and 2024 presidential candidate, Ramaswamy's star appeal among conservatives led to quick backing by Ohio Republicans and hopes of an easy victory in the Republican-dominated state. However, despite a massive fundraising lead and more than $12 million spent in campaign advertising, he is now locked in a close fight with Acton with weeks to go until Election Day."I'm so grateful to this state and to this country for giving a kid like me opportunities that would not have been available to my family in any other country on planet earth," Ramaswamy said at the rally ahead of Trump's arrival, as he underscored the American dream for his Indian immigrant family.

news.title: Tankers Hit Near Strait of Hormuz as Oil Prices Stay Near $100 Despite G7 Reserve Release
news.text: At least three tankers have been struck by unidentified projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz since October 1, even as the G7 announced a large release of emergency oil to ease high fuel prices. Brent crude is hovering around $100 a barrel. The UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO) says the attacks mark a sharp jump in strikes on commercial shipping. Early on Saturday, a crude oil tanker was hit on its port side about 4 nautical miles east of Oman. That followed two incidents on Friday. One outbound ship suffered a small fire and lost power, and a second crude tanker was hit close by. On Thursday, Iran's Fars news agency said a supertanker carrying 2.5 million barrels caught fire off Oman. Fars said the ship was using an unauthorized route. Iran's version of eventsIranian state media, citing the Persian Gulf Strait Authority, says seven tankers were targeted over five days. It named three ships as repeat violators: AL RUWAIS, SINBAD and MERSIN PROSPERITY. Tehran claims all three are owned or chartered by the United Arab Emirates. State broadcaster IRIB also reported that a tanker exploded in the strait. Its sources said the ship had turned off its tracking system on entering the waterway. Last Tuesday, Revolutionary Guard spokesman Brigadier General Hossein Mohebbi warned that any vessel crossing without Iran's permission could be attacked or could hit a mine. Washington pushes backU.S. Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth rejected Iran's claim of control. "They don't control it, we do," he said, adding that Iran has "literally gotten nothing through." He described the American blockade as "ironclad" and said traffic is running almost at pre-war levels every night. G7 opens its emergency stocksPrices are the other big worry. The G7 agreed to release emergency oil and diesel over several months after pressure from President Donald Trump. The war on Iran and Russia's war on Ukraine have both pushed up energy costs. In a joint statement after a video call chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron, the group said it would coordinate a release of 100 million barrels through the International Energy Agency (IEA). The release starts right away and runs for four months. It includes a large diesel release in the first 20 days, and leaders will discuss more diesel relase if needed. The statement did not say how much each member will contribute. Other steps in the plan: G7 refineries will coordinate maintenance schedules so they do not shut down at the same time.Refineries will temporarily run at higher rates where possible.Member countries are urged not to put export limits on energy products among themselves.Earlier in the week, the Trump administration had threatened to ban U.S. diesel exports and pressed Europe to release its emergency diesel. Why diesel is so expensivePrices have jumped sharply. Oil rose by more than $4 a barrel on Thursday. The American Automobile Association (AAA) says the average U.S. price of diesel reached a record $6.50 a gallon last Friday, up from $5.61 a month before. Neil Atkinson, a former IEA oil markets official, told Al Jazeera that three things are squeezing supply. Little diesel is moving from the Middle East to Europe, which had relied on Saudi Arabia and Kuwait. Russia has stopped exporting diesel altogether after Ukrainian attacks on its refineries. And China has stopped exports too. Meanwhile, demand is staying high because of the harvest season. The U.S. is the world's largest diesel producer and exporter, shipping about 1.26 million barrels a day, according to JODI and OPEC data. Russia ranks second among exporters at 783,400 barrels a day. Will it work?Macron said the release will "bring down the prices" of petroleum products, especially diesel. Markets gave a mixed reaction. Brent briefly fell below $100 after the announcement but climbed back to about $102 in the evening.
news.summary: At least three tankers have been struck by unidentified projectiles in and around the Strait of Hormuz since October 1, according to UKMTO warnings. Meanwhile, the G7 has agreed to release 100 million barrels of emergency oil, but Brent crude is still hovering around $100 a barrel.

news.title: What happened at Cornell University? The allegations, conflicting accounts and probe now underway
news.text:
APAn intense outcry followed a woman's allegations of gang-rape at a Cornell fraternity house.

An intense, public outcry over a woman's account of being gang-raped at a Cornell University fraternity house prompted New York's governor this week to angrily yank control of the investigation away from the local prosecutor who didn't initially see what happened as a crime.Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has said Cornell police omitted key information that could have affected his decision whether or not to pursue criminal charges.Also Read: New York governor appoints special prosecutor in Cornell fraternity rape caseNow, the task of unraveling the case will fall to the state's attorney general, Letitia James, who was appointed as a special prosecutor.James, a Democrat best known for tangling with President Donald Trump, suggested at a news conference Friday that her investigation wouldn't be rushed. She described it as a monthslong process, with no predetermined outcome.Live EventsHere's what we know and don't know about the woman's allegations and the investigations that followed:A lawsuit shone a fresh light on the woman's allegationsThe woman sued Cornell and seven former students last month, alleging she was given ketamine and became completely incapacitated while members of the Chi Phi fraternity sexually assaulted her at their campus residence in October 2024.She reported the alleged assault to campus police about three weeks later, giving investigators a detailed account over two days. She also spoke with Cornell's disciplinary investigators.But Van Houten quickly declined to pursue charges or further investigation after reviewing a police summary of her interview.After the victim filed her civil suit, Van Houten said it contained allegations he had never seen. He contended Cornell's police had withheld key information, including a transcript of the woman's interview where she explicitly said she was "100% confident" she was raped.Van Houten said the materials suggested she had consented to some sex with multiple men, hadn't been forced into other acts, and was intoxicated, but not to the point of helplessness.Under New York law, being too drunk or high to consent to sex isn't necessarily enough to support a rape charge. The law distinguishes that from being physically helpless or incapacitated by drugs administered without consent.Also Read: Kathy Hochul, Letitia James give major update on Cornell University Sexual Assault probeVan Houten later reopened the investigation. "Seeking justice sometimes requires us to reconsider or reopen cases when we are provided with additional evidence," he said.The school's investigation produced conflicting accountsOnly a fraction of the evidence collected by the school has become public, but the portions that have provided a fuller - though disputed - timeline of events, as well as a glimpse at how the men responded to being accused.According to the records, the woman had been invited to the fraternity by a member for whom she had long held strong romantic feelings. Cornell's disciplinary panel found that she initially consented to sex with that man and one of his friends, though she later alleged in her lawsuit that she had been pressured into taking drugs and alcohol and was too intoxicated to consent.Later, other men started coming into the room, some drawn by a message one of the fraternity brothers sent to a Snapchat group at 1:42 a.m. using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available.The woman told investigators that her intoxication had rendered her partly defenseless. She said some of the men inhaled drugs off her unclothed body."I felt like bait. I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in," she told investigators.The records also show that she acknowledged that her memory of the night was spotty, due to her extreme inebriation, and had verbally acquiesced to some acts she later felt were sexual abuse.Some of the accused men disputed her account when speaking to investigators, or said that the drug use and sexual activity were consensual.Cornell hasn't detailed the results of its investigation, but said it resulted in some students being expelled. The records show it also cleared at least some of the men of sexual assault allegations.New York's governor was outraged by the police investigationHochul said she appointed James because she had lost faith in Van Houten's handling of the case. She said Van Houten should have asked Cornell for more information and interviewed the woman before closing it."This woman, this young woman, had already endured something that is utterly unspeakable," she said. "And then at every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her."Van Houten said he supports James' appointment but maintains that New York law didn't allow him to prosecute based solely on the woman's allegations that she was too incapacitated to consent.The case sparks calls for changeAt a Cornell Student Assembly meeting Thursday, students and other members of the university community spent more than 2 1/2 hours discussing the handling of sexual assault allegations. Some expressed fear, anger, and grief - while others shared their own experiences of sexual violence on campus.Among them was Jane Wang, who said she had reported being sexually assaulted at Cornell a year earlier.When she filed her Title IX case in the midst of "mental, physical and emotional recovery from the assault," she said, "I was also met with an abundance of paperwork, very little instruction on how to navigate it and no follow-up from our Title IX office of an outcome."The presidents of every fraternity in Cornell's Interfraternity Council voted unanimously to cancel social events this weekend in response to the allegations, according to The Cornell Daily Sun. Twenty student organizations are also planning a protest Monday to voice support for a promised independent review of Cornell's handling of the case and advocate changes to its sexual assault policies, the newspaper reported.In a video message Saturday, Cornell President Michael Kotlikoff pledged greater transparency amid the mounting outrage about how the school handled the case. He called the gang rape allegations "deeply disturbing" and said the case would weigh on the university for years to come.The case has also renewed scrutiny of a New York sexual assault law that makes it more difficult to prosecute cases involving people too intoxicated to consent. New York is one of 19 states with such laws.Hochul said Friday that she supports changing the law.Add as a Reliable and Trusted News Source Add Now!

news.title: Lettuce probe into largest foodborne illness outbreak of parasite in US history: Mexico's Health Ministry investigation finds shocking results
news.text:
ReutersFarm workers seen through shimmering heat while working on a lettuce farm near Salinas, California, U.S. (Reuters photo)

Mexico's Health Ministry said on Saturday that a US Food and Drug Administration investigation into the cyclospora parasite outbreak linked to shredded iceberg lettuce from Taylor Farms in Mexico did not conclusively identify the source of contamination. Mexico's food-safety regulator Cofepris said tests conducted by its national reference laboratory on raw materials, finished products and water from the facility investigated in the outbreak were negative for the cyclospora parasite.The regulator added that environmental findings alone do not constitute conclusive evidence that agricultural products were the source of contamination. The FDA said on Friday it found a strong epidemiological and traceback link between the outbreak and recalled shredded iceberg lettuce produced by Taylor Farms in Mexico, but said there was insufficient evidence to determine how contamination occurred.The agency reported two environmental samples positive for cyclospora in Mexico, one from wastewater leaving a processing facility and another from a drainage ditch at an iceberg lettuce farm. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention declared the outbreak over on September 11. The outbreak sickened 12,883 people in 21 states, hospitalized 570 and was linked to two deaths.Mexico said it cooperated throughout the investigation, providing traceability information, inspections and samples, and would continue technical cooperation with US health authorities.The Food and Drug Administration said on Friday that its inspectors detected cyclospora at the Mexican farm blamed for the largest foodborne illness outbreak of the parasite in U.S. history.Live EventsYou Might Also Like:Daylight Saving Time: Donald Trump makes cell phone number of Republican Senator public over Sunshine Protection Act. What is the debate all about?Despite the finding, the FDA said it’s unclear how the parasite got into lettuce at Taylor Farms’ facility. The agency has now closed its investigation into the outbreak, which led to nearly 13,000 cases of diarrhea and other illnesses across the U.S.The announcement comes more than six weeks after the agency sent its investigators to the farm in Guanajuato, Mexico. The visit was the agency’s first time there in more than seven years following a steep drop in international food safety inspections after the COVID-19 pandemic.FDA inspectors said Friday they found cyclospora in two places: a wastewater tank and a drainage ditch used for lettuce cultivation. While it’s unclear how the contamination took place, the FDA said the samples provide “strong epidemiological data” linking the outbreak to the Taylor Farms site.Cyclospora is a microscopic parasite that commonly causes watery diarrhea “with frequent and sometimes explosive bowel movements,” according to the CDC. news.title: Iran's IRGC hit 7 'violating' oilers in Hormuz Strait in 5 days
news.text: Digital Desk | Tehran, Oct 4 (IANS) The navy of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) has targeted at least seven "violating" oil tankers in the Strait of Hormuz in the past five days, the semi-official Fars news agency reported. The IRGC Navy has targeted more than one oil tanker each day, despite US President Donald Trump's repeated claims that "the Strait of Hormuz is open and under his country's control," it reported. Citing MenchOsint, an independent military observer, Fars added that two oil tankers were exploded in the Strait of Hormuz on Friday -- one at the waterway's entrance and the other while exiting it. MenchOsint also said that two Kuwaiti tankers, Al FUNTAS and KAZIMAH III, and three United Arab Emirates vessels, SINBAD, MERSIN PROSPERITY and AL RUWAIS, were struck in the strait over the previous four days, reports Xinhua news agency. Meanwhile, Trump on Saturday said that the war with Iran would end “very quickly” and predicted oil prices would fall sharply once the conflict was over, as he portrayed Tehran as militarily and economically weakened. Speaking to reporters after arriving in Texas and later during a visit to a Peterbilt Motors facility in Denton, Trump said Iran faced a choice over how the conflict would end. “Iran will very soon be ending one way or the other,” Trump told reporters. “It'll either just say, look, they have 301 percent inflation. They have no money, they have no currency. Their military has been defeated, their navy is gone, their air force is gone, everything's gone.” “And, one way or the other, it's going to end very quickly. And when that ends, oil prices are going to drop like a rock,” he said. Iran tightened its grip on the Strait of Hormuz on February 28, barring safe passage of vessels belonging to or affiliated with Israel and the United States following their joint strikes on Iranian territory.

news.title: Trump Says US Will Decide on Iran, Warns of 'Easy or Hard Way'
news.text: Washington DC: US President Donald Trump on Saturday (local time) said that Washington will take a decision on Iran, stating that the outcome would come either the "easy way or the hard way", while asserting that Iran has been "decimated". "We have a decision that I'll make about Iran. Iran's been decimated. So the only question is, it'll either be the easy way or the hard way. We'll have it the easy way or the hard way," Trump said to reporters outside the White House. Trump's remarks came as he continued to withhold details of his forthcoming actions concerning Iran, while saying that the situation was progressing favourably and that Iran was not doing well. Speaking to reporters on Friday, Trump, when asked about his upcoming strategy regarding Iran, initially suggested that revealing his plans would generate significant headlines. "If I told you, you'd have a major story, right? But you'll see. Working out very well. Iran is not doing well," Trump said. The US President did not provide further details about potential administration measures or a timeline for his next steps. Earlier, Trump said that the war with Iran would conclude "very quickly" and forecast a sharp decline in oil prices once the hostilities ended, while describing Tehran as heavily degraded economically and militarily. Speaking to reporters in Texas, Trump said Iran faced a decisive choice over how the conflict would end. "Iran will very soon be ending one way or the other," Trump said. "It’ll either just say, look, they have 301 per cent inflation. They have no money; they have no currency. Their military has been defeated, their navy is gone, their air force is gone, everything's gone," he added. "And, one way or the other, it’s going to end very quickly. And when that ends, oil prices are going to drop like a rock," the US President further stated. Trump's latest remarks come amid continued US pressure on Iran, with preventing Tehran from obtaining a nuclear capability remaining a cornerstone of US policy.

news.title: Brazil’s Lula and Bolsonaro close campaigns ahead of critical election  | Barbados Gazette – Barbados &
news.text:
Brazilian President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and right-wing Senator Flavio Bolsonaro have wrapped up their election campaigns, each voicing confidence in victory ahead of Sunday’s tightly contested first-round presidential vote.

Lula, 80, closed his re-election bid on Saturday with a march through Sao Paulo, Brazil’s economic powerhouse, drawing what his campaign called a record crowd for a closing rally.

“Tomorrow, we’re going to win the elections in the first round,” he told supporters, describing Sunday’s vote as a choice between “democracy and barbarism” and promising to “defeat the far right”.

He has also framed the election as a test of Brazil’s sovereignty, warning against “meddling” by Washington.

Bolsonaro led a motorcycle caravan through towns in Sao Paulo state, echoing the campaign style of his father, before rallying later in Rio de Janeiro. “I am convinced that everything is in place for us to win this election in the first round,” he said.

The 45-year-old is the son of former President Jair Bolsonaro, a close ally of US President Donald Trump. The former leader, 71, is serving a 27-year prison sentence for attempting to overturn his 2022 election loss to Lula.

The younger Bolsonaro was photographed at his rally holding a portrait of his father.

Trump has not formally endorsed Bolsonaro but has said he is watching the election “very closely”, a level of US interest that has become a flashpoint in the campaign.

Lula’s supporters have seized on it as evidence Washington is trying to meddle in the elections, while some Bolsonaro supporters, frustrated by the cost of living, say they would welcome US pressure if it helped force change at home.

Polls released on Saturday suggested Lula was still ahead but his lead was narrowing, with neither candidate likely to win outright on Sunday. Such a result would send the race to a run-off on October 25 between the two frontrunners, a contest polls suggest would also be close.

It is a far tighter race than Lula’s last victory in 2022, when he beat the elder Bolsonaro by less than two percentage points.

Meanwhile, the Bolsonaro campaign has faced scrutiny over a film-funding scandal. Flavio Bolsonaro is under investigation over financing for Dark Horse, a biopic about his father, bankrolled by a jailed banker tied to one of Brazil’s biggest financial scandals.

Brazil’s Supreme Court authorised federal police in April to investigate whether Flavio Bolsonaro made defamatory statements about Lula.

Bolsonaro has pledged to seek his father’s release from prison if elected, and has echoed his father’s unsubstantiated claims questioning the reliability of Brazil’s electronic voting system, which analysts say could be laying the groundwork to contest the result if he loses.

Beyond the presidency, Brazil’s nearly 160 million registered voters will also choose lawmakers, governors and senators on Sunday.

Right-wing candidates have gained ground in Latin America in recent months.

news.title: Yemen's Armed Forces Bomb Sanaa and Saada, Houthis Retaliate With Strike on Oil Facility Near Riyadh
news.text: Yemen's armed forces said on Saturday that they are carrying out strikes against Iran-aligned Houthi forces in the capital, Sanaa, and the group's stronghold of Saada. The two sides have traded strikes since last month, when the Houthis launched a lightning offensive, seizing all of Yemen's Red Sea coast and taking control of the Bab al-Mandab strait. This comes after Houthis said they had attacked a major oil facility in Saudi Arabia with ballistic missiles and drones. The claim came after flames and a large plume of smoke were seen rising from the Aramco refinery on Saturday, and firefighters tackled the blaze. A spokesperson for the forces, which are aligned with Yemen's internationally recognised government, said they were targeting "vital targets" but gave no further details. The Houthi-run Al Masirah television channel earlier reported what it said was a Saudi air attack on Sanaa. Saudi Arabia has not immediately confirmed the report. Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said the group had targeted an oil facility in Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, and that the attacks had set the targeted sites ablaze. The AFP journalist saw firefighters trying to put out a fire at Aramco's Riyadh refinery, south of the capital. Ambulances and police vehicles were stationed nearby. Fighting Spreads The conflict between the Iran-backed Houthis and forces aligned with the Saudi-backed government has intensified as part of the wider war between Iran and the United States. Hostilities resumed this year after the Houthis declared a naval blockade on Saudi Arabia in July and began attacking Saudi territory and shipping. The Houthis have also made significant territorial gains along Yemen's Red Sea coast, including areas near the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait. Saudi Arabia has responded with air strikes in Yemen while backing government forces fighting the Houthis. The Houthis said on Saturday that they had attacked an oil facility near Riyadh with ballistic missiles and drones, claiming that the strikes caused fires. An AFP journalist reported seeing flames and smoke rising from an Aramco facility south of the Saudi capital, although Saudi authorities have not commented. Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV also reported that Saudi aircraft had carried out 26 strikes on Sanaa. Two correspondents in the city said they heard loud explosions and saw warplanes firing missiles. Fighting Returns After Years of Calm Yemen's civil war pits the Iran-backed Houthis, who control most of the country's north-west including Sanaa, against the internationally recognised government, which is based in Aden and controls much of the south and east. The latest escalation followed the arrival of an Iranian plane in Sanaa carrying a Houthi delegation. The flight did not seek Saudi authorisation, contravening a practice that had been in place for a decade. Saudi Arabia responded by striking Sanaa airport, after which the Houthis launched attacks on Saudi territory for the first time since 2022. Since then, the Houthis have seized coastal territory along the Bab al-Mandab strait and attacked Saudi targets, including oil infrastructure and sites around Riyadh. They have also announced a naval blockade of Saudi shipping in the Red Sea. The renewed fighting has added to Yemen's already severe humanitarian crisis. The World Food Programme warned on Friday that three-quarters of the country's population was unable to meet its basic food needs. Fighting has also intensified around Taiz, where sources on both sides reported dozens of combatants killed on Friday. The Houthis said 55 of their fighters had been killed, while government sources told AFP that 26 troops had died. The Houthis have captured territory around Taiz but have not taken the city itself, Yemen's third-largest after Sanaa and Aden. Saudi authorities have also reported that a Houthi projectile damaged a school in Najran, near the Yemen border. Riyadh has reportedly sought US assistance, but US President Donald Trump has so far declined to provide it. US news outlet Axios reported on Saturday that senior members of the Trump administration had met to discuss Yemen and the wider Iran conflict, citing three US officials.
news.summary: The conflict has drawn in regional dynamics, with Iran backing the Houthis and Saudi Arabia responding with airstrikes

news.text: TEHRAN: The United States has "kicked out" two members of the Iranian delegation who attended the recent UN General Assembly after they ignored an order to leave the country, the State Department said Saturday."Two more members of the Iranian delegation were found still in (New York) long after the United Nations General Assembly had passed.
